**Surat Muhammad (ﷺ)**

It is also called **Surat al-Qital** (the Chapter of Fighting). According to most scholars it is Madani (Medinan), and they mention no exception. However, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah report that it is Madani except for the verse ﴿And how many a town﴾ to the end of the verse, which was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) left Makkah for the cave. He turned toward it and said: "You are the dearest of God's lands to God, and you are the dearest of God's lands to me. Had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left you."

God then revealed that verse. On this basis the surah would be Makki (Meccan), taking as Makki (Meccan) in the technical sense whatever was revealed on the road to Madinah before the Prophet (ﷺ) reached it, that is, what was revealed during the journey of the Hijrah (migration). This is supported by a report that 'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi transmitted with his chain of narration to Yahya ibn Sallam.

The number of its verses is forty according to the Basran count, thirty-eight according to the Kufan count, and thirty-nine according to the count that uses the letter *ta'* with two dots above it (the Basran? no, the count that reads ﴿ladhdhatin lil-sharibin﴾ with *ta'*). Thirty is the count according to all others. The disagreement concerns the verses ﴿until war lays down its burdens﴾ and ﴿a delight to the drinkers﴾.

The connection between the beginning of this surah and the end of the surah before it is clearly strong and tightly woven. If the basmalah were removed between them, they would read as one continuous text without any discord, like a single verse, each part holding onto the neck of the other. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it in the Maghrib (sunset) prayer, as al-Tabarani reported in al-Awsat from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Surat Muhammad was revealed, one verse about us and one verse about the Banu Umayyah." I do not think this report is sound. Yes, the disbelievers of the Banu Umayyah have the greatest share of the general verses that concern the disbelievers, just as the Ahl al-Bayt, may God be pleased with them, have al-Mu'alla and al-Raqib among the general verses that concern the believers. Nothing more than this should be said, except that I say: May God curse whoever cuts off the ties of kinship and harms the family of the Prophet.

**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of God﴾: that is, they turned away from Islam and from following its path, or they prevented others from it. This is on the basis that *sadda* (to bar) may be intransitive or transitive. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "The first is more apparent, because barring from the way of God is turning away from what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, as in God's words: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God﴾. This matches God's words: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾. Many reports, however, support the second meaning." Al-Dahhak interpreted ﴿the way of God﴾ as the House of God, and said: "Barring them from it means preventing those who intend it." But this is not correct.

The verse is general, applying to everyone who is characterized by the description in the relative clause. Ibn 'Abbas said that those meant, in the second sense of *sadda* (barred), were the feeders on the day of Badr al-Kubra (the Great Battle of Badr). It seems he meant those who fall primarily within the scope of the verse, since those people barred with their wealth and their persons, so their barring is greater than the barring of others who disbelieved and barred from the way. The first of those who fed people, according to what is reported from the biography of Ibn Sayyid al-Nas, was Abu Jahl, may the curse of God be upon him, who slaughtered ten camels for the disbelievers of Quraysh when they set out from Makkah. Then Safwan ibn Umayyah slaughtered nine at 'Usfan. Then Suhayl ibn 'Amr slaughtered ten at Qudayd. Then Shayba ibn Rabi'ah slaughtered nine, when they had lost the way. Then 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah slaughtered ten. Then Miqyas al-Jumahi slaughtered nine at al-Abwa'. Then al-'Abbas slaughtered ten, and al-Harith ibn 'Amir slaughtered nine. Abu al-Bakhtari slaughtered ten at the water of Badr, and Miqyas [slaughtered] nine. Then the war occupied them, and they ate from their provisions. It is also said there were six men: Nabih and Munabbih, the two sons of al-Hajjaj; 'Utbah and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'ah; and Abu Jahl and al-Harith, the two sons of Hisham. Muqatil added six others to them: 'Amir ibn Nawfal, Hakim ibn Hizam, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. Each of them fed the Ahabish and the troops for one day, while they relied upon them to fight the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Counting Abu Sufyan among those [feeders], if the report is sound, does not contradict his being with the caravan, because "the day of Badr" refers to the time of the battle, so it includes those who fed on the road and throughout its duration until it ended. Muqatil said: "They were twelve men from among the people of polytheism who used to bar people from Islam and command them to disbelieve." It is also said: "They were devils from among the People of the Book, who barred whoever among them or others wished to enter Islam."

The relative clause is the subject, and its predicate is God's words: ﴿He has made their deeds go astray﴾. That is, He nullified and annulled them and made them lost, without effect and without any benefit at all. This does not mean that He nullified and annulled them after they had been otherwise, but that He, mighty and majestic, decreed their nullity and loss. What is meant by them is the deeds of righteousness they used to do, such as maintaining ties of kinship, hospitality to guests, freeing captives, and other noble deeds.

It is also permitted that the meaning is: He made them misguidance, that is, not guidance, since He did not grant them success in intending His face by them. Or He made them *dallah* (straying), that is, not guided, by way of metaphorical attribution. Whoever says the verse concerns the feeders and their like says: the meaning is that He, majestic and exalted, nullified what they did of scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), such as the spending they made on their journey to wage war against him, peace and blessings be upon him, and other things, by granting victory to His Messenger (ﷺ) and making manifest his religion over every religion. This is perhaps more fitting with what follows it, and likewise with what has been said, that the verse was revealed at Badr.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 2:

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said, as related from him by a group of narrators including al-Hakim, who authenticated it, that they are the people of Madinah, the Ansar. May Allah be pleased with him, he explained ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ as the people of Makkah, the Quraysh. Muqatil said: they are some people of the Quraysh. It was also said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. And it was said: it is more general than what has been mentioned and others, since the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is among the forms of generality (sighat al-'umum), and there is no reason to restrict it. ﴿And believe in what has been sent down to Muhammad﴾, namely the Qur'an. Belief in this was singled out for mention, although it is included in what precedes it, to honor its status and to draw attention to its lofty position among all that must be believed in, and because it is the foundation of everything. For this reason it was emphasized by His saying, ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾. This is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridah) between the subject and the predicate, serving to restrict truthfulness to it in the manner of restriction found in His saying, ﴿That is the Book﴾, and in your saying, "Hatim is the generous." Thus "the truth" is meant as the opposite of falsehood. It is also permissible that the restriction be taken in its apparent sense, meaning the established truth, and that what was sent down to him, upon him be prayers and peace, is true because it is abrogating and not abrogated (naskh: abrogation). This requires that it be given attention, and for this reason emphasis came. In any case, His saying ﴿from their Lord﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in "the truth". Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Muqsim read (nuzzila) in the active voice. Al-A'mash read (unzila), with the causative hamza, in the passive voice. It was also read (anzala) with hamza in the active voice, and (nazala) with lightened pronunciation.

﴿He expiated from them their misdeeds﴾, meaning He covered them with faith and righteous deeds. What is intended is that He removed them and did not hold them accountable for them. ﴿And He set right their state (bal)﴾, meaning their condition in religion and in worldly life, through success and support. The interpretation of (bal) as "condition" (hal) is related from Qatadah. It is also related from him that it is interpreted as "affair" (sha'n), which is also a condition, or as "that which has importance". Al-Raghib's statement agrees with this: "al-bal is the condition about which one cares, and for this reason one says, 'ma baliytu bi-kadha' (I did not care about such-and-such), meaning I was not concerned with it." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every matter of importance (dhi bal) [is begun with the praise of Allah]", the hadith.

It may also mean the inward thought (al-khatir al-qalbi), and it is used figuratively for the heart, as al-Shihab said. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): the literal meaning of bal is thought (fikr), and the place where a person's attention rests, which is the heart. Whoever's heart is sound, his condition is sound. So the wording seems to point to the soundness of their belief, and other conditions follow from it. It is reported from al-Safaqsi that he interpreted it here as thought, and perhaps this is for the reason indicated. It is also said in al-Bahr that it is among the words that are not dualized nor pluralized, and the plural form "bālāt" that some use is anomalous (shadh).

**﴿ذَلِكَ﴾** is a reference to what has preceded: the misguidance, the expiation, and the setting right. It is the *mubtada'* (subject, الْمُبْتَدَأ) whose *khabar* (predicate, الْخَبَر) is the statement of God, exalted is He: **﴿بِأنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا اتَّبَعُوا الباطِلَ وأنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اتَّبَعُوا الحَقَّ مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾** ("because those who disbelieved followed falsehood, and because those who believed followed the truth from their Lord"). That is, this occurs because of the first group's following of falsehood and the latter group's following of the truth. By "the truth" and "falsehood" is meant their well-known meanings.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid the interpretation of **(al-Batil)** (falsehood) as Satan. In *al-Bahr* (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is related that Mujahid said: "Falsehood is Satan and everything that he commands. **﴿والحَقَّ﴾** (and the truth) is the Messenger and the Law." It has also been said: falsehood is that from which no benefit is derived.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that **﴿ذَلِكَ﴾** be the *khabar* of an omitted *mubtada'* (a deleted subject), and that **﴿بِأنَّ﴾** and what follows is in a position of *nasb* (accusative, مَحَلّ نَصْب) as a *hal* (circumstantial clause, الحال). The sense is: "The matter is that," i.e., as mentioned, being connected with this cause.

The governing element of the *hal* is either the meaning of the demonstrative (الإشارة) or a word such as *athbituhu* ("I establish it") or *ahaqquhu* ("I affirm it"), since the sentence implies that, because it is the content of every statement. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it involves an unnecessary deletion (ارْتِكابًا لِلْحَذْفِ مِن غَيْرِ داعٍ). The prepositional phrase **(min rabbihim)** ("from their Lord") is in the position of a *hal* in every case. The utterance, namely God's words **﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّ﴾** up to His words **﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾**, is an explicit statement of what the preceding speech implied concerning causation, because it is built upon the relative pronoun (المَوْصُول). The scholars of rhetoric (عُلَماء البَيان) call this *al-tafsir* (explanatory elaboration). A parallel to it is what al-Zamakhshari recited of his own verse:

*"By it the horsemen were stricken above their steeds,*
*as the unmarried maidens were stricken behind the curtains.*
*The swords fell from their hands in bewilderment,*
*and the necklaces shook loose from their necks."*

In it there is an explanatory elaboration in the manner of *al-laff wa al-nashr* (the folding and unfolding device, اللَّفّ والنَّشر), as in the verse, and it is among the excellences of speech.

**﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾** (Thus), i.e., like that wonderful form, **﴿يَضْرِبُ اللَّهُ﴾** (God presents / sets forth), i.e., makes clear, **﴿لِلنّاسِ﴾** (for mankind), i.e., for their sake, **﴿أمْثالَهُمْ﴾** (their parables), i.e., the conditions and attributes of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, which run in strangeness in the manner of proverbs. These are: the believers' following of the truth and their success and prosperity, and the disbelievers' following of falsehood and their loss and ruin.

It is also permitted that the striking of parables means representation and comparison, in that God, exalted is He, made the following of falsehood a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, misguidance a parable for their ruin, the following of truth a parable for the deeds of the believers, and the expiation of misdeeds a parable for their success. The demonstrative **﴿بِذَلِكَ﴾** refers to what the preceding speech contained. It is also permitted that the pronoun in **(amthalahum)** ("their parables") refers to mankind.

The fa' in His saying ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve﴾ indicates the sequencing of the command contained in what follows it upon what precedes it. The misguidance of the disbelievers' deeds, their frustration, and the goodness of the believers' conditions and their success necessitate that each side be subjected to the rulings that befit it. The meaning is: since the matter is thus, then when you meet them on the battlefield, ﴿strike at the necks﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Laqitum" is from "liqa'" (encounter), which means fighting, and "darb" (striking) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) for an omitted verb. The original is "idribu al-riqab darban" (strike the necks with a striking). The verb was omitted, the verbal noun was placed first, and it was made to substitute for the verb while being annexed to its object. Omitting the governing verb in such a construction, when the verbal noun is annexed to its object, is obligatory. It is one of the cases in which omission is required, mentioned in the lengthier books of grammar. It is not among them, however, in cases like "darban Zaydan," as Ibn 'Usfur stated explicitly.

Many scholars have mentioned that this includes brevity and emphasis. There is no dispute about brevity. As for emphasis, the apparent implication of this view is that the verbal noun, after its governing verb is omitted, is emphatic. Al-Himsi said in the margins of al-Tasrih: the verbal noun in such constructions is emphatic originally, but not now, because it has become like the verb it has replaced. Thus it is not emphatic. Rather, every verbal noun that has become a substitute for the verb in pronunciation is neither emphatic nor specifying of a type or a number. "Darb al-riqab" is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for killing. It is expressed by this to indicate that it should be by striking the neck wherever possible, and to depict it in the most hideous image, because striking the neck involves severing the head, which is the noblest of the body's members and the gathering place of its senses, while the body is left lying in a repugnant state, and we seek Allah's refuge. It has also been mentioned that in this expression there is encouragement of the believers, and that they are of such a kind that they are able to kill by striking their necks in battle.

﴿Until when you have subdued them﴾: that is, you have inflicted killing upon them with severity and abundance. This is figurative, taken from the thickening (thakhn) of liquids, because it prevents them from movement. The intended meaning is: until, when you have increased their killing and become able to take those who were not killed. ﴿Then bind them firmly﴾: that is, take them captive and keep them secure. The binding and what follows it apply to those among them who were taken captive after being subdued, not to the one who has been subdued, since in the earlier sense he is not bound, nor is he granted freedom, nor is he ransomed, because he has already been killed. Or the meaning is: until, when you have weighed them down with wounds and the like so that they cannot rise, then take them captive and keep them secure. In this case the binding and what follows apply to the one who has been subdued, because in this sense he is the one who has not reached the point of being killed, but has become too heavy to move, so he is like a thick thing that has not flowed and has not continued in its course. "Ithkhan" in this sense is also figurative. "Al-wathaq" (the binding) is originally a verbal noun like "al-khalas," and it is used here to mean that by which one is bound. It has also been read as "al-wathaqi" with a kasra, and it is a noun for that. The occurrence of the pattern "fi'al" as an instrument noun, like "al-hizam" and "al-rikab," is rare and contrary to analogy. The apparent sense of some scholars' statements is that each of the fathah and kasrah forms is a noun for that by which one is bound, and perhaps the purpose here is to clarify the intended meaning.

﴿Then either grace afterward or ransom﴾: that is, either you grant them grace, or they are ransomed by ransom. The statement is an elaboration of the outcome of the content of what precedes it, namely binding. The omission of the verb governing the verbal noun in such a construction is also obligatory, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I will surely strive, so either the repelling of a calamity that is feared, or the attainment of the aim and hope."

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that each of "mannan" and "fida'an" be an object of an omitted verb, meaning: grant them "mannan," or accept from them "fida'an." Abu Hayyan said that this is not a grammatical analysis (i'rab). Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, read "wa-imma fada" with a fathah and without the madd, like "'asa." Abu Hatim claimed that it is not permissible to read it without the madd, because it is the verbal noun of "fadaytuhu." Al-Shihab said: there is no weight to this claim, for there are four dialects for it: fathah and kasrah with madd and qasr, and a fifth dialect, which is indeclinability with kasrah, as reported by the trustworthy transmitters, ended. In al-Kashf, citing al-Sihah, it is stated: "al-fida'" when its first letter is kasrah is read with madd or qasr, and when it is fathah it is qasr. Some Arabs use kasrah on the hamzah, meaning they make it indeclinable on kasrah specifically when it exceeds the preposition lam, because it is a verb-noun with the meaning of supplication. Al-Asma'i recited the verse of al-Nabighah: "Gently, may I be ransomed for you." This kasrah is with tanwin, as clarified in al-Bahr.

According to what al-Suyuti mentioned in Ahkam al-Qur'an al-'Azim, the apparent meaning of the verse is the prohibition of killing after capture, and al-Hasan held this view. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: al-Hajjaj brought captives, and he handed a man to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, to kill him. Ibn 'Umar said: "We were not commanded with this. Allah the Exalted only said: ﴿Until when you have subdued them, then bind them firmly; then either grace afterward or ransom﴾."

There is disagreement concerning the ruling on captives. Most scholars held that the Imam has the choice: if he wishes, he may kill them if they do not embrace Islam, because the Prophet (ﷺ) killed by way of execution 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it, Tu'aymah ibn 'Adi, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, about whom his sister said verses, among them addressing the Prophet (ﷺ):

"What would it have cost you had you shown grace? Often a youth shows grace though he is enraged and furious."

Also, killing them removes the root of their corruption entirely. It is not permitted for any one of the warriors to kill a captive on his own. If he does so without compelling cause, such as fear of the captive's harm, the Imam may discipline him if the act was contrary to the intended purpose, but he does not owe any compensation. If the Imam wishes, he may enslave them, because in that there is a repelling of their harm together with great benefit to the people of Islam. If he wishes, he may leave them as free protected persons (dhimmi) for the Muslims, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did with the people of al-Sawad. Except for captives from the idolaters of the Arabs and apostates, for jizyah is not accepted from them, and their enslavement is not permitted. Rather, the ruling concerning them is either Islam or the sword. If captives embrace Islam after capture, he does not kill them, since their harm is averted by Islam, but it is permitted to enslave them, for Islam does not negate slavery as a punishment for original disbelief, which has occurred after the cause of ownership has been established, namely seizure of a non-idolatrous enemy from among the Arabs. This is unlike the case where they embrace Islam before being taken, for they are then free, because it is Islam before the cause of ownership has been established over them.

Ransoming captives is not permitted, according to one of the two narrations from Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, because it involves aiding disbelief, since the captive disbeliever returns to be a combatant against us. Repelling the harm of his hostility is better than rescuing a Muslim, because if the Muslim remains in their hands, his affliction is confined to himself alone, whereas the harm of returning their captive to them falls upon the whole community of Muslims.

The other narration from him is that ransoming is permitted, and this is the view of Muhammad, Abu Yusuf, Imam al-Shafi'i, Malik, and Ahmad, except that ransom with women is not permitted according to them. Ahmad prohibited ransoming with their children. This is the narration of al-Siyar al-Kabir. It is said that this is the more apparent of the two narrations from Imam Abu Hanifah. Abu Yusuf said: ransoming captives is permitted before division of the spoils, not after. According to Muhammad, it is permitted in every state.

The reasoning of the imams who mentioned the permissibility of ransom is that freeing a Muslim is preferable to killing a disbeliever, because of the benefit of him, and because his sanctity is great. As for the harm mentioned that returns to us by returning them to the enemy, it is apparently removed by the Muslim who is freed from them, because it is the harm of one individual, and one like him stands to repel it apparently, so they are equal, and the virtue of freeing a Muslim and enabling him to worship Allah the Exalted remains, for in it there is an added preponderance.

Then, this has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir reported from 'Imran ibn Husayn that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ransomed two men from the Muslims for one man from the idolaters. Muhammad's view is supported by what Muslim also reported from Iyas ibn Salamah, from his father Salamah, who said: "We went out with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had appointed as commander over us," and he went on to say: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me the next day in the market and said: 'O Salamah, give me the woman,' meaning the one whom Abu Bakr had given him as a reward. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, she has pleased me, and I have not uncovered any garment for her.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me the next day in the market and said: '(O Salamah, give me the woman, for Allah's sake, may your father be bereaved)'. I said: 'She is yours, O Messenger of Allah. By Allah, I have not uncovered any garment for her.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent her, and with her he ransomed some Muslims who had been captured in Makkah."

Ransoming a captive who has embraced Islam while he is still in our hands is not permitted, because it is not valid unless his soul is content, and he is trusted regarding his Islam. It is permitted, because it frees a Muslim without harming another Muslim. As for ransoming with property, it is not permitted according to the well-known view of the Hanafi school, for the reason explained in the ransoming of Muslims, namely returning them as combatants against us. In al-Siyar al-Kabir it is stated that there is no harm in it if the Muslims have a need. It is said as evidence: the captives of Badr, for there is no doubt about the need of the Muslims, indeed about the severity of their need at that time. Therefore, let the interpretation of the ransoms that took place at Badr be ransom with property.

As for granting grace to captives, which is releasing them to the abode of war without anything in return, it is not permitted according to Abu Hanifah, Malik, and Ahmad. Al-Shafi'i permitted it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) granted grace to a group of the captives of Badr, among them Abu al-'As ibn Abi al-Rabi', as reported by Ibn Ishaq with his chain, and Abu Dawud from his path to 'Aishah: "When the people of Makkah sent to ransom their captives, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for the ransom of Abu al-'As with property, and sent with it a necklace which Khadijah had given her on the occasion of her marriage to Abu al-'As. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw that, he was greatly moved by it and said to his companions: 'If you see fit to release her captive for her and return to her what belongs to her,' and they did so, rejoicing in it." Al-Hakim narrated it and declared it authentic, and he added: "(The Prophet (ﷺ) had taken a pledge from him that he would send Zaynab to him, and he did so)." The Prophet (ﷺ) also granted grace to Thumamah ibn Uthal ibn al-Nu'man al-Hanafi, the chief of the people of Yamamah, after which he embraced Islam and his Islam was excellent. His hadith is in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah. It is sufficient what is established in Sahih al-Bukhari of his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "(Had al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi been alive and then spoken to me about these foul ones, meaning the captives of Badr, I would have left them to him.)" He (ﷺ), who is truthful and whose truthfulness is attested, informed that he would release them if al-Mut'im asked him. Release on that hypothetical basis would not be established except if it were permissible under the law, given the infallibility of the Prophet. That it did not occur, because what was conditioned upon it did not happen, does not negate its permissibility under the law.

The verse under discussion has also been cited as evidence, for Allah the Exalted gave the choice in it between grace and ransom. The apparent meaning of grace is release without payment. That the intended meaning is granting grace to them by abandoning killing and leaving them enslaved, or allowing them to accept the jizyah and be among the protected people, contradicts the apparent meaning. Some souls find the taste of blessings sweeter than this grace.

Some Hanafi scholars answered that the verse has been abrogated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Kill the idolaters wherever you find them﴾ from Surah Bara'ah, for it requires the impermissibility of grace and likewise the impermissibility of ransom. That verse is the last surah revealed on this matter. They claimed that what occurred of grace and ransom was in the case of Badr, which is prior to it. And if anything of that occurred after Badr, it too is before the surah.

The view of abrogation (naskh) is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Mujahid, in narrations that al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentions in al-Durr al-Manthur. The great scholar Ibn al-Humam said: "It may be said that this (i.e., what is in Surah Bara'ah) concerns those other than the captives, on the evidence that it is permissible to enslave them. Thus it is known that the killing commanded applies to others than them. What he mentioned about the permissibility of enslavement is not absolute, for, as you know, it is not permissible to enslave the polytheists of the Arabs."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 47, verse 8:**

﴿And those who disbelieve, [for them is] *fa-ta'san* (تَعْسًا) — destruction⁠⁠—﴾ From *ta'isa al-rajul* (تَعَسَ الرَّجُلُ), with the vowel of the ʿayn opened, *ta'san* (تَعْسًا), meaning he fell on his face. Its opposite is *intaʿasha* (انْتَعَشَ), meaning he got up from his fall. Shamir, Ibn Shumayl, Abu al-Haytham and others said: *ta'isa* with the ʿayn vowel closed (تَعِسَ). It is said: *ta'san lahu wa-nukusan* (تَعْسًا لَهُ ونُكْسًا), where, as Ibn al-Sikkit said, the first means falling on the face and the second means falling on the head. Al-Himmasi, in his glosses on al-Tasrih, said: *ta'isa ta'san* means he did not get up from his stumble. *Nukusan* (نُكْسًا) is with the nun vowelled with *damma*, though it may also be opened, either in a rare dialect or by imitation of *ta'san*. *Al-nukus* (النُّكْسُ) with *damma* means the return of an illness after recovery. This is used as a supplication, and it was common to say *ta'san lahu* as a curse against the one who stumbles. In supplication for him one says *la'a lahu* (لَعا لَهُ), meaning raising him up and making him stand. They cited the verse of al-Aʿsha describing a she-camel:

*I burdened her, an unknown self of mine, and my concern supported me upon her whenever she was exhausted and stood still,*

*with a camel of strong gait, sturdy, when she stumbles—so ruin is better for her than my saying "la'a".*

Tha'lab and Ibn al-Sikkit also said: *al-ta'is* (التَّعِسُ) is destruction. From this is the verse of Majma' ibn Hilal:

*She says, after I had separated her from her husband: "You are ruined as you have ruined me, O Majma'."*

In al-Qamus: *al-ta's* (التَّعْسُ) is destruction, stumbling, falling, evil, distance and decline. The verb is in the pattern of *manaʿa* and *samiʿa*, or, when you address someone, you say *ta'ista* (تَعِسْتَ) with the pattern of *manaʿa*, and when you report it you say *ta'isa* (تَعِسَ) with the pattern of *samiʿa*. It is said: *ta'asahu Allah* and *at'asahu*, and a man is *ta'is* and *taʿis*. Its accusative status is as an absolute object (مَصْدَر) governed by a verb of the same root that must be omitted, because it is used for supplication, like *suqyan* and *ra'yan*. Thus it follows the pattern of proverbs when used in this sense. The prepositional phrase *lahu* after it is, according to many, connected to a implied element to clarify it, meaning "I mean for him a proverb." So for *ta'san lahu* there are two clauses. The Kufans held that it is a single sentence. Ibn Hisham has a discussion about this prepositional phrase, mentioned in the section on the *lam* of clarification, so consult it there.

The expressions differ regarding the interpretation of this noble verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means distance for them. Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi said: it means grief for them. al-Hasan said: it means reproach for them. Ibn Zayd said: it means misery for them. al-Dahhak said: it means humiliation for them. Al-Naqqash related its interpretation as ugliness for them. Many others said: it means stumbling and decline for them. How graceful is the mention of this regarding them after the mention of the firming of feet regarding the believers. In a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, he meant in this world death, and in the Hereafter falling headlong into the Fire. Most of the statements return to supplication against them for destruction.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted two possibilities in its grammatical analysis (iʿrab). The first is that it is an absolute object of an omitted verb, as already mentioned. The second is that it is an object of an omitted verb, meaning "so He decreed destruction for them." On the first, he took the verb to be *qawl* (saying), meaning "so He said: destruction for them." What prompted him to this, as it is said, is making *alladhina* (الَّذِينَ) the subject, with the sentence joined by *fa* (الفاء) as its predicate, and that sentence is an invocation (إنشاء الدعاء). An invocation cannot be a predicate without interpretation, so either a *qawl* is implied with it, or it is made a predicate by implying *qada* (قضى). His statement, exalted is He, *"and He misguided their deeds"* (﴿وأضَلَّ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾), was taken as coordinated with what was implied.

In al-Kashf: what is meant by "he said: destruction for them" is that Allah destroyed them, not that there is an actual supplication and speech. This is because one does not invoke a curse upon a person unless he deserves it, so when the Exalted informs that He invokes it against him, it indicates that destruction is certain, especially since the apparent meaning of the words is that the supplication is from Him, glorified and exalted. This is a metaphor upon a metaphor, meaning that the saying is metaphorical, and likewise the supplication with *ta'san* is metaphorical. The coordination was not made with *ta'san* because it is a supplication, whereas "and He misguided" (وأضَلَّ) is a report. Even if it were made a supplication also, coordinated with *ta'san* according to the aforementioned figurative usage, it would have a valid basis. End of quotation. You know that the consideration Zamakhshari took into account is not only for the sake of coordination, but also for the sake of the informative character. If it is held that informing by an invocative sentence is valid without interpretation, then one can dispense entirely with what he said. The *fa* entered into the predicate of the relative pronoun because it includes the meaning of a conditional.
