It is also permitted that the relative clause be in the accusative position as the object of an implied verb, which the following accusative word (*ta'san*) explains: meaning "Allah made those who disbelieve fall into ruin" or "Allah made those who disbelieve fall, a fall," in accordance with what you have heard from al-Qamus, and this has been related from Abu ʿUbayda. The *fa* is then extra in the speech, as in the verse ﴿and your Lord, so magnify﴾ (﴿ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ﴾). The Arabs add it in such cases, imagining a condition. It was also said: the verb is implied as a present tense verb coordinated with His statement ﴿He strengthens﴾ (﴿يُثَبِّتُ﴾), meaning "and He causes to fall those who..." etc. The *fa* is then for coordination, so the meaning is causing ruin after ruin, and its parallel is His statement ﴿and Me, so fear Me﴾ (﴿وإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾). Or it is because the explainer (المفسِّر) should be mentioned right after what is explained, like detail after summary. There is a discussion about this.

This is Alusi's commentary on verse 9 of Surah Muhammad (47).

﴿That﴾, i.e., what was mentioned of ruin and misguidance, ﴿is because﴾, by reason of the fact that, ﴿they disliked what Allah has sent down﴾ of the Qur'an, because of what it contains of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the other rulings that oppose what they were accustomed to and what their souls commanding evil (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su') desired. This is a specification and an explicit statement that disbelief in the Qur'an is the cause of ruin and misguidance, since it is already known from His words, exalted is He, ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, etc., that general disbelief is the cause, and disbelief in the Qur'an enters into it primarily. ﴿So He made fruitless﴾, on account of that, ﴿their deeds﴾, which, had they done them along with faith, they would have been rewarded for. The mention of nullification (al-ihbat) alongside misguidance, the latter being what is intended by it, indicates that disbelief in the Qur'an necessarily entails it and is never separated from it in any way.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 10:

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth⁠﴾, i.e., they were made to sit in their places and so did not travel through it. ﴿And see what was the end of those before them⁠﴾ from the disbelieving nations. For the traces of their dwellings tell of their histories. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God destroyed them⁠﴾ is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "What was their end?" So it was answered: what belonged to them of self, family and wealth was destroyed. One says *dammarahu* (دَمَّرَهُ), meaning "he destroyed him," and *dammara 'alayhi* (دَمَّرَ عَلَيْهِ), meaning "he destroyed what belonged to him." So *dammara 'alayhi* is more emphatic than *dammarahu*. The emphasis comes from omitting the object and making it "a forgotten thing forgotten" (*nasyan mansiyyan*), and from using the preposition *'ala* (عَلَى, "upon"), because destruction here includes the meaning of falling upon, attacking, or the like. ﴿And for the disbelievers⁠﴾, i.e., for these disbelievers who follow their way, ﴿there are similar ones⁠﴾, similar to their end or their punishment, by the indication of what preceded it. But this does not mean that these people will receive similar things to those of the former people, or multiples of them, but rather their equivalent. The plural is used in view of its being similar to many ends, according to the number of nations punished. It has also been said: it is possible that their punishment is harsher than the punishment of the earlier ones, since they were killed and taken captive at the hands of those whom they used to despise and oppress. Killing at the hands of one's equal is harsher than destruction by a general cause. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is the earlier ones, by way of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, as if it were said: God, exalted is He, destroyed them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter there are similar ones.

ذَلِكَ (Dhalika, "that"): a demonstrative referring to the establishment of the like of the outcome or punishment of the earlier nations for these people. It was also said that it refers to victory, though, as you see, this is weak. ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector (mawla) of those who believed﴾, meaning, their Helper against their enemies. It is also read (waliyyu alladhina amanu, "the Ally of those who believed"). ﴿And that the disbelievers have no protector﴾, so He repels from them what has befallen them of punishment and torment. This is not contradicted by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Mawla (Master)﴾, because the mawla there carries the meaning of owner, so the negation and the affirmation do not fall upon one and the same meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ This is an explanation of the ruling of His guardianship (wilayah) over them, exalted is He, and its otherworldly fruit. ﴿But those who disbelieve enjoy themselves﴾, that is, they benefit from the goods of this world for a few days. ﴿And eat as cattle eat.﴾ The kaf (ka, "as") is in the accusative position. It may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the verbal noun (masdar), as Sibawayh says, meaning: they eat it, that is, the eating, resembling the eating of cattle. Or it may be a qualifier (na't) of an omitted verbal noun, as most grammarians (mu'rabun, those who discuss i'rab, grammatical analysis) say, meaning: eating like the eating of cattle. The meaning is that their eating is stripped of thought and reflection, just as one says to an ignorant person, "You live as the beast lives," not intending a comparison in the mere fact of living, but in its properties and necessary features. Its essence is that they eat heedless of their outcomes and the end of their affairs. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire is their abode﴾, that is, their place of dwelling, is a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the waw of (ya'kuluna, "they eat").

It is also permitted that it be a new sentence (isti'naf). In that case His saying, exalted is He: ﴿enjoy themselves and eat﴾ stands in opposition to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, because of what it implies: that they recognized that the bliss of this world is a vain illusion and a passing shadow, so they abandoned the desires and devoted themselves to righteous deeds, and their end was everlasting bliss in a noble station. As for these, they were heedless of that and frolicked in their filth like beasts, until abandonment (khidhlan) drove them to their resting place in the depths of the Fires. This is what the scholar al-Tibi mentioned in explaining the opposition between the two verses. Some eminent scholars said: there is ihtibak in the speech (a rhetorical device in which an element is omitted from each of two parallel parts, each part supplying what is missing in the other). That is, the righteous deeds and entry into the Garden were mentioned first, as evidence for the omission of the corrupt deeds and entry into the Fire second; and the mention of enjoyment and abode second is evidence for the omission of scant provision and shelter first. The first is better and more subtle. He attributed the entry into the Garden to Allah, exalted is He, and did not follow this same course in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the Fire is their abode﴾. The two clauses are varied as verbal and nominal, to signal the precedence of mercy, to inform of the destiny of the believers, and to promise that their end is that Allah, glorified is He, admits them into gardens, while the disbelievers' abode is the Fire, and they are now present therein without awareness, and like cattle they eat.

﴿Wa-ka'ayyin﴾ is in the sense of *kam* (how many) used for information (*khabariyyah*), and it is the subject (*mubtada'*). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿min qaryah﴾ (from a town), is its specification (*tamyiz*). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿hiya ashaddu quwwatan min qaryatika﴾ (it is stronger in might than your town), is an adjective (*sifah*) of *qaryah*, just as His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿allati akhrajatka﴾ (which expelled you), is an adjective of *qaryatika*. The genitive (*mudaf*) has been omitted from both, and its rulings have been applied to them, as the predicate (*khabar*) clarifies, which is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ahlaknahum﴾ (We destroyed them). The meaning is: "And how many people of a town, who are stronger in might than the people of your town who expelled you, We destroyed them with various kinds of punishment." It is also permitted that there is no omission here, and that the place is intended while its inhabitants (*al-hal*) are meant metaphorically. The attribution of the expulsion to the people of his town (ﷺ), which is Makkah the Honoured, is a metaphor by way of attributing the act to its cause (*al-isnad ila al-sabab*), because they treated him (ﷺ) with what they treated him with, and so they were the cause of his expulsion when Allah, exalted is He, permitted him (peace be upon him) to emigrate from it. A parallel to this is the expression "Bring me to your land, I have a right over you" (*aqdimni baladaka haqqun li 'alayk*).

You know that, according to what the eminent scholars (*al-ajillah*) have verified, it admits of three aspects: a metaphor in the attribution (*majaz fi al-isnad*), if *al-iqdam* (bringing/arriving) is used in its literal meaning for which it was coined, even if it is imagined; a metaphor in the locative (*majaz fi al-tarf*), if it is used in the sense of causing to arrive (*al-haml 'ala al-qudum*); and a metaphorical allusion (*isti'arah bi al-kinayah*), if *al-haqq* (the right) is used in the sense of the one who precedes. The Shaykh says regarding such cases: the transitive verb is imagined and has no agent, so that the attribution to it is literal; thus there is no real *iqdam* (advancing) in the intention of the speaker, but rather the depiction of arrival in the form of advancing, and attributing it to the right depicted in the form of one who precedes is an exaggeration of its being a summoner to arrival. Al-Sialkuti approved this in the marginal notes to the commentary on the *Mukhtasar al-Talkhis* and defended it against *qal wa qil* (idle disputation). The full discussion is there, and the discussion of the verse is in the same vein.

The description of the first town with intense might serves to indicate that the second is more deserving of destruction because its might is weak, just as the description of the second with its expulsion of him (peace be upon him) serves to indicate that it is more deserving of it because its crime is grave. In the same manner is the verse of al-Nabighah:

*Kulayb, by my life, was more numerous in helpers and lighter in crime than you, (he) was drenched in blood.*

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-la nasira lahum﴾ (so they have no helper), explains that they cannot be rescued through helpers and supporters, following the explanation that they cannot be rescued from Him by themselves. The *fa'* (so) is for ordering the mention of what is by others after the mention of what is by themselves. It is a narration of a past state, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-aghshaynahum fa-hum la yubsirun﴾ (so We covered them, and they cannot see). We do not accept that the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) does not function literally in the past tense. The verse is a consolation for him (ﷺ). Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Prophet (ﷺ) left Makkah for the cave, he turned towards Makkah and said: "You are the most beloved of Allah's lands to Allah, and you are the most beloved of Allah's lands to me. Had your people not expelled me from you, I would not have left you."

So the worst of enemies is the one who transgresses against Allah, exalted is He, in His sanctuary, or who kills someone other than his killer, or who kills by the entry of the people of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*). Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed ﴿wa-ka'ayyin min qaryah﴾ and so on. What relates to this has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah, so reflect on it.

Page 47

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 14:

﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ is a statement establishing the contrast between the condition of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, and that the former are in the highest ʿIlliyyin while the latter are in the lowest of the low (asfal safilin), and it is an explanation of the cause of the state of each of them. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying that the two are equal, or for denying that the matter is other than as has been mentioned. The fa' (particle) is for conjunction upon an implied premise required by the context, and it has been read without it. And (man, "one who") is an expression for the believers who hold fast to the proofs of the religion, just as it is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made appealing﴾, where it is an expression for their opposites among the polytheists.

A group has related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord" is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made appealing" refers to the polytheists. Something similar has been related from Qatadah, and al-Zamakhshari went to this view. It has been criticized that such restriction is not supported by the noble composition nor is there any reason for it. It was said: similar to this is that the first (man) is an expression for him (ﷺ) and for the believers. The meaning is: Are the two groups equal, or is the matter not as has been mentioned? So is one who stands firm upon a manifest proof and a luminous demonstration from the Lord of his affair, who nurtures him, namely the Great Qur'an and the rest of the miracles and rational proofs, like one for whom Satan has made appealing his evil deed of polytheism and the rest of the sins, such as your expulsion from your town, though that is in itself the worst of the vile deeds. ﴿And they followed﴾ in that evil deed, and it was said: by reason of that adornment, ﴿their desires﴾, the deviant ones, without there being for them any doubt that would make them think that what they are upon is correct, let alone a proof that would indicate it to you. The pronouns in the last two were pluralized in view of the meaning of (man), just as the singular form of the first two is in view of its wording.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 15 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ to the end of the verse is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that serves to describe the excellences of the Garden promised to the believers just previously, and to explain the manner of its rivers, the flowing of which beneath it was indicated. He referred to them as "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqun) to signal that faith and righteous deeds fall under taqwa, which is the doing of obligations and the abandoning of misdeeds. The word "mathal" (parable) means a remarkable description, and it is the subject (mubtada') by the agreement of the grammarians. They differed over its predicate (khabar). It is said that it is omitted. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: its estimate is "what you hear." God's words ﴿In it are rivers﴾ to the end of the verse explain it. Sibawayh said: its estimate is "what is recited to you," or "what We have related to you," and it is estimated as preceding. "In it are rivers," etc., is an explanation of that parable. Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it as "apparent in the mind of whoever comprehends these attributes," but that is not the case. Perhaps the most suitable estimate for the beginning of this noble text is that of al-Nadr. It is also said that the predicate is stated, namely God's words ﴿In it are rivers﴾ etc., with the meaning: "the parable of the Garden and its description is the content of this statement," and such an excellence does not need a connecting pronoun.

It is also said that this sentence is the predicate, except that the word "mathal" is a superfluous addition, like the addition of a noun in the saying of one who said:

"Until the year's end, then the greeting of peace upon you both."

So the subject in reality is the genitive complement, and it is as if it were said: "The Garden: in it are rivers, etc." But this is nothing.

It is also said that the predicate is God's words that come later:

[p. 48]

﴿like one who abides in the Fire﴾, and God willing, a full discussion of this will come.

Ali, may God ennoble his face, and Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah, and al-Sulami read (amthal al-Jannah), i.e., its attributes. Ibn Jinni said: this is evidence that the reading of the majority with the singular means plurality, because "mathal" carries the meaning of a verbal noun (masdar). That is why one says: "I passed by a man like two men," "and by two men like men," and "by a woman like a man." It is also reported from Ali, may God ennoble his face, that it was read (mithal al-Jannah). The "mithal" of a thing is, originally, its counterpart with which it is compared.

﴿of water unchanging﴾, i.e., not changed in taste and smell due to long standing and the like. Its past tense is asina, with fatha, from the pattern of darab and nasar, and with kasra from the pattern of 'alima. Al-Khafaji reported this from the lexicographers. In al-Bahr: "The water became asin," i.e., its smell changed; it is yasan and yasin. Tha'lab mentioned this in al-Fasih. The verbal noun is usun. "Asina" with kasra in the present is "yasna" with fatha, the dialect of "asina," as stated by al-Yazidi. "Asina al-rajul" with kasra only, when a man enters a well and a foul smell from it reaches him, so he faints or his head spins. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I shall leave the horn with yellowed fingertips, swaying in the wind like the sway of a drawer of water who is overcome by foul air."

Ibn Kathir and the people of Mecca read (asin) on the pattern of hadhir, so it is an adjectival form (sifah mushabbahah) or an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah). He read (yasin) with the letter ya'. Abu 'Ali said: this is with the hamza lightened.

﴿and rivers of milk whose taste does not change﴾, i.e., it has not turned sour, nor become sharp or tart like the milks of this world. Change of smell does not separate from change of taste.

﴿and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾, i.e., pleasant to them. There is no unpleasantness of taste or smell, no harm from intoxication, and no headache, unlike the wines of this world, for there is no pleasure in the drinking itself, and it contains what it contains of disagreeable and harmful things. The word (ladhdhah) is the feminine of the adjectival form ladhdh, and it is applied to wine because wine is feminine, although it may also be masculine. Or it is a verbal noun described by it, with an omitted modifier implied, or by making the thing itself the pleasure, for emphasis, as is well known in such expressions. It is read in the nominative, as an attribute of (rivers), and in the accusative, as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning "existing for the sake of pleasure, not for anything else, such as headache and the other afflictions of the wines of this world."

﴿and rivers of honey, clarified﴾, which is not mixed with what would alter it, so wax and the excrement of bees and other things are not mixed into it. Its description as "clarified" is because clarity is the characteristic most prevalent in honey. Honey is of the kind that is both masculine and feminine, as Abu Hayyan and others stated. This, as it has been said, is an illustrative image for what in Paradise corresponds to drinks, with every kind of what is agreeable, or what is pleasant in this world, by purification from what diminishes or spoils it, and by embellishment with what brings abundance and permanence.

Water is mentioned first because in this world it is what one cannot do without; then milk, since it serves as food for many Arabs at many times; then wine, because when quenching and eating are achieved, the soul yearns for what gives pleasure; then honey, because in this world it is a cure for what affects drinks and food, so it comes later in rank. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the milk of those rivers was not milked. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it did not come out from between dung and blood; its wine was not trodden by men's feet; its honey did not come out of the bellies of bees. Ibn Jarir reported from Sa'd, who said: I asked Abu Ishaq about God's words ﴿of water unchanging﴾, and he said: I asked al-Harith about it, and he told me that this water is Tasnim. He said: I was told it is not touched by any hand, and that the water comes like this until it enters the mouth.

In a hadith reported by Ibn Mardawayh from al-Kalbi: the river Tigris is the river of wine in Paradise, and over it is Abraham, peace be upon him; the river Jayhun is the river of water in it, and it is called the river of the Lord; the river Euphrates is the river of milk, and it belongs to the descendants of the believers; and the river Nile is the river of honey.

Al-Harith ibn Abi Usama in his Musnad and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ka'b, who said: The Nile is the river of honey, the Tigris is the river of milk, the Euphrates is the river of wine, and the river Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise. You know that what is mentioned in the verse is rivers in the plural in general, and God knows best the soundness of these reports and the like. Then, if they are sound, their interpretation is not far-fetched, although divine power cannot be frustrated by anything.

[p. 49]

﴿And for them therein﴾, together with what has been mentioned of the various kinds of rivers, ﴿from all the fruits﴾, i.e., kinds of all the fruits. The prepositional phrase is a description of an omitted subject. Some estimated it as "pairs," apparently deriving this from God's words ﴿In both of them, of every fruit, two kinds﴾. It is also said that "min" is superfluous, i.e., "for them therein is every fruit." ﴿And forgiveness﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, i.e., "for them is forgiveness." It is also permitted that it is conjoined to the earlier subject without the qualifier "therein," because forgiveness precedes entry into Paradise, or with the qualifier, and the statement is with an omitted modifier, i.e., "and the bounty of forgiveness," or by making forgiveness a designation for its effect, which is bounty, or metaphorically for the good pleasure of God, mighty and majestic. It may be said that forgiveness here means the covering of their sins and not mentioning them to them, lest they feel shame and their pleasure be spoiled. The earlier forgiveness means the covering of sins and the non-punishment for them, and then the conjunction is to the subject without any of what was mentioned. I have seen something similar after writing this, in al-Tabarsi, who limited himself to it, and perhaps it is better than what they said. The indefiniteness of (forgiveness) is for magnification, i.e., a great forgiveness whose measure cannot be estimated. God's words ﴿from their Lord﴾ are connected to an omitted attribute of it, emphasizing by the added specification the majesty that the indefiniteness conveys, i.e., "originating from their Lord."

God's words, mighty and majestic, ﴿like one who abides in the Fire﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "Is one who abides in this Garden, as the promise has run, like one who abides in the Fire," as God's words attest: ﴿and the Fire is their abode﴾. It is also permitted that it is an apposition to God's words, glorified is He: ﴿like one whose evil deed is made attractive to him﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthesis to explain what distinguishes one who is upon clear proof in the Hereafter, as confirmation of the denial of equality; but this is remote. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) went to the view that it is the predicate of ﴿the parable of the Garden﴾, and that this is governed by the preceding denial, namely God's words ﴿Is then he who was﴾ etc. The meaning is: "Is the parable of the Garden like the recompense of one who abides in the Fire?" So the two genitives are omitted: "recompense" by the context of the contrast with the Garden, and the word "parable" by its prior mention. Similar cases are many. The reason for omitting the particle of denial is that whoever is confused about the first, namely the state of one who holds to clear proof and the state of one who follows his desire, then the second is the same as the first in his view, and in that case he does not deserve to be addressed. A parallel to this is the saying of Hadrami ibn 'Amir:

"I rejoice that the noble should be bereaved, and that I should inherit a she-camel with a slender tail, of noble stock."

This is a statement denying joy at the loss of the noble and the inheritance of the camel, while lacking the particle of denial, because it is subsumed under the ruling of one who said to him: "Do you rejoice at the death of your brother and at the inheritance of his camels?" This is of the kind of acquiescence under which every denial is diminished.

God's words ﴿In it are rivers﴾ have been treated as a kind of repetition of the relative clause, i.e., a relative clause after a relative clause, which includes its detailed description, because it is like the detail of what was promised. For this reason the conjunction did not come between them. It is also permitted that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), on the basis that the adverbial phrase occupies the position of that, and ﴿and rivers﴾ is its agent (fa'il), not that it is a subject with the adverbial phrase as a fronted predicate. A nominal clause as a circumstantial clause without a waw is in this case, and they have stated that the sufficiency of a pronoun in it is not eloquent. Taking it as a verbal clause by estimating the verb of the adverbial phrase as "established" is not hidden in its state. It was said that the circumstantial clause is weak in meaning because it comes in the manner of supplements, and this is the mother of denial. Also, it is a circumstantial clause of "the Garden," not of its pronoun in the relative clause, and in the governing element there is contrivance. Then the circumstantial clause is not restricted, and making it emphatic, although its being so is known from God's report in it, is also contrived. It may be the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is an explanatory resumption, said al-Kashshaf: "This is the proper view, and the estimate is: 'It is: in it are rivers,' as if it were said: 'How can it be an attribute of the Garden when it is such-and-such, like the attribute of the Fire?' The resumption here is in the position of your saying: 'and it is such-and-such,' a parenthetical statement to what is implied by the word 'parable' of the wonderful description. The predicate of the earlier clause, namely ﴿like one who abides in the Fire﴾, is not the object of a question to be objected to by the occurrence of the resumption before its completion." It was objected that there is no need to estimate a subject, because ﴿In it are rivers﴾ is a clause in itself. The answer is that the estimate is "like it: in it are rivers." So the genitive complement was omitted and the one who is genitive replaced it, becoming nominative, then was omitted. That is why he said in the question: "as if someone said: 'And what is like it?'" The same applies to the reading of the Commander of the Faithful, may God ennoble his face and that of those with him, (amthal) in the plural, so it is said: the estimate is "the parables of the Garden are like the parables of the recompense of one who abides in the Fire," and the first genitive complement is estimated as plural for agreement. But by my life, Jar Allah has gone far from the aim, and many of the verifiers have approved what he mentioned. The author of al-Kashf said after establishing that ﴿like one who abides﴾ is the predicate of "the parable of the Garden": "This is the apparent and suitable way of the context."

Ibn al-Munir said in al-Intisaf after quoting him: "However many views people have stated concerning the interpretation of this verse, I have not seen anything more smooth or sweet than these subtleties he mentioned. It only lacks the note that there is an omitted element in the sentence to make it balanced. The estimate is: 'the parable of the inhabitants of the Garden is like one who abides in the Fire.' Of this type is God's words: ﴿Have you made the watering of the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque like one who believes in God﴾ etc. What we have estimated to achieve balance is better, even if it involves more omission. So reflect on this, and may God, exalted, guide you." The singular pronoun, i.e., (huwa), refers to (man) in view of its wording, just as the plural pronoun in His words, glorified is He: ﴿and they are given water boiling﴾ refers back to it in view of its meaning. The intended meaning is "and they are given boiling water in place of those drinks," and in this there is mockery of them. ﴿So it cuts their bowels﴾ due to the excess of heat.

It is related that when it is brought near to them, it scalds their faces, and the skin of their heads comes apart; and when they drink it, it cuts their intestines to pieces. The word (أمعاءهم) is the plural of (مِعًى), pronounced with either a fatha or a kasra, and it refers to what food passes into after the stomach. It is also called (عَفاج), which is masculine, though it may sometimes be treated as feminine.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 16:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ — they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). The singular pronoun is used in accordance with the wording (lafz), just as the plural that follows is used in accordance with the meaning (ma'na). Ibn Jurayj said: "They used to attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and would hear his words but would not retain them, nor would they observe them with their proper observance, out of their own negligence." ﴿Until, when they go out from you, they say to those who have been given knowledge﴾ — that is, to the people of knowledge among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). It has also been said that "those who have been given knowledge" refers to those who retain his words and observe them with their proper observance among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). ﴿What did he say just now?﴾ — that is, what did he say just before this time? Their intention in this was mockery, even though it took the form of inquiry. It is also permissible that their intention was a genuine inquiry, if they did not give him their ears out of negligence toward him, and for this reason they were blamed. The first view is preferable. It has been said that this was said concerning Ibn Mas'ud. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "I am one of them, and I have been named among those who were asked," meaning that he is among those who "have been given knowledge" by the explicit text of the Qur'an. How excellently this is expressed.

(Ā'nifan) is an active participle (ism fa'il) contrary to analogy, or it is derived by stripping its verb of its augmentations, since no triliteral verb for it has been heard; rather, one says ista'nafa and ata'nafa. al-Zajjaj mentioned that it is from istanafa al-shay' ("he began the thing") when one initiates it, and that the original sense of this is "I took its nose," i.e., its beginning. The original meaning of anf (nose) is the well-known organ, and then the term is applied to the extremity, front, or most noble part of a thing. Many scholars mentioned that ānifan derives from this: they said it is a noun for the hour immediately preceding your present hour, from anf in the sense of "what comes before," and it has been borrowed from the organ because of its precedence over the present time. It has also been said that it means the time of the present state, and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who held that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time. That it is an active participle does not preclude its use as an adverb, just as in bādi' (beginning), which is an active participle that in usage has come to take the sense of an adverb of time. But Abu Hayyan said: "The correct view is that it is not an adverb of time, and we know of no grammarian who counted it among the adverbs of time, and he required that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of (qala), i.e., 'what did he say beginning (mubtadi'an)?' meaning: what is the speech that he has just now begun, before we separated from him?" And the words of al-Raghib point to this. Ibn Kathir read (anifan) on the pattern fa'il. ﴿Those⦆ — the ones described by what has been mentioned — ﴿are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾, so they did not turn toward good; ﴿and who followed their desires﴾, so they turned toward everything in which there is no good. Therefore there came from them what came.

﴿Those who are guided﴾ to the path of truth, ﴿He increases﴾ (i.e., God, exalted and majestic is He) ﴿in guidance﴾ through enabling grace (tawfiq) and inspiration (ilham). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") may be in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), or in the accusative governed by a verb omitted and explained by the mentioned verb. ("Guidance," hudan) is the second object (maf'ul thani), since zada (to increase) can take two objects. It may also be a specifying accusative (tamyiz). The first is the more apparent. Its tanwin (nunation) indicates magnitude, i.e., "a great guidance." ﴿And He gave them their God-consciousness﴾ (taqwahum), i.e., He gave them their taqwa (God-consciousness) from Him, may He be glorified, by creating it in them, according to what the Ash'arites say about the acts of servants, or by creating in them a power over it that effectively produces its act by His permission, may He be glorified, as al-Kūrānī attributed to al-Ash'arī and the other verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) concerning the acts of servants: that they are by a power God, exalted is He, created in them, effective by His permission, exalted is He. The statement of some of them, that He made them, may He be glorified, God-conscious toward Him, may be applied to either of the two views. Al-Bayḍāwī said: that is, He made clear to them what to beware of, or helped them toward their God-consciousness, or gave them its reward. So the giving (iytha') is, in his view, a metaphor for clarification or help, or it is literal and taqwa is a metaphor for its reward, since it is its cause, or there is an omitted genitive construction (mudaf muqaddar). Nothing in any of these contradicts the doctrine of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq). Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned the second and third of these. Al-Ṭībī preferred the first of these two and said: it is more harmonious with the composition of the noble text, because most verses of this noble surah are arranged in antithesis (muqabalah). Thus ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God has sealed﴾ is matched with His words, may He be glorified: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾, because sealing results from the accumulation of rust and the repeated succession of what increases disbelief. And His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they followed their desires﴾ are matched with His words, majestic is He and exalted: ﴿and He gave them their God-consciousness﴾. So it is interpreted as the perfection of taqwa, which is that the knower (al-'arif) purifies himself from whatever occupies his inner self (sirr) away from the Truth, and devotes himself entirely to Him, may He be glorified, with all his being (bashara shara'ir). This is the true taqwa intended by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Fear God as He should be feared﴾. For the increase upon an increase of guidance is an increase beyond which there is no increase. In rising above following desire is the yearning toward the Master and the detachment from the pleasures of the lower life. Then, in attributing the giving of taqwa to Him, exalted is He, and attributing the following of desire to them, there is an allusion to the meaning of His words, exalted is He, in narration: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, and a hint that following desire is a spiritual sickness, while persistence in taqwa is a divine remedy. End of quotation. What he mentioned of antithesis applies to what we have mentioned as well. Likewise, antithesis also holds on the interpretation of giving taqwa as clarifying what they should beware of, because the discourse indicates that what they are upon is not the pursuit of desire and caprice, but a true matter founded on a strong basis. The interpretation of it as giving the reward of taqwa is narrated from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, and al-Jubba'ī adopted it. The discourse on this is more beneficial and further from emphasis, without any need to take taqwa in its highest degrees. The matter of antithesis is simple, for it may be said that His words, exalted is He, ﴿those who are guided﴾ correspond to ﴿they followed their desires﴾, and His words, may He be glorified, ﴿He increased them in guidance﴾ correspond to ﴿God sealed their hearts﴾. So let this be pondered. It was also said: the subject of (zadahum, "He increased them") is the pronoun referring to the Prophet (ﷺ), understood from His words, exalted is He, ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ and His words, may He be glorified: ﴿What did he just say?﴾. Likewise the subject of (atahum, "He gave them") is the same, i.e., he helped them or clarified for them, and the attribution is metaphorical. It is not hidden that this contradicts the apparent sense. Also, if His words, exalted is He, ﴿He increased them in guidance﴾ correspond to His words, may He be glorified, ﴿God sealed their hearts﴾, then it is better that its subject be the same as the subject of the latter, and that the rest proceed similarly according to what al-Ṭībī said, lest there be a disjunction. It was also permitted that the pronoun refer back to the statement of the hypocrites, for that is among things at which the believer marvels, so he praises God, exalted is He, for his faith and increases in insight into his religion. But this is very far-fetched, indeed hardly worth considering.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So do they await anything but the Hour?﴾ That is, the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that it come upon them suddenly﴾ means: that it surprise them suddenly, and suddenness (al-mufaja'ah) is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "the Hour." That is, they do not take heed of the conditions of the earlier nations, nor of the reports of the coming of the Hour and of the great tremendous events in it. So they await nothing for taking heed except the coming of the Hour itself. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for its portents have already come﴾ means: its signs (alamat) and indications (amarat), as in the verse of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali:

"If you have resolved to cut off between us,
then you have made the portents of its beginning appear."

Ashrat is the plural of shart (with a vowel on the shin and a sukun on the ra'), and this is the reason for its suddenness, in the sense that there remains among the matters that necessitate taking heed no matter awaited that they await except the coming of the Hour itself, since its portents have already come. So they did not pay it any attention and did not count them among the beginnings of its coming, so its coming will necessarily be by way of suddenness. Thus it is in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim. The apparent sense of the words of al-Kashshaf is that it is a reason for the coming in general, that is, they await nothing but the coming of the Hour because its portents have already come, and after their coming the Hour must occur. Giving a reason for the qualified element without its qualifier is not free of remoteness. It was said: what brings this closer here is that their waiting is only for the coming of the Hour, and qualifying it with suddenness is only to clarify the reality. Some of the verifiers said: it is a reason for waiting for the Hour, because the appearance of the signs of a thing is a cause of waiting for it. In making it a reason for suddenness there is obscurity, because suddenness does not fit the coming of the portents except by interpretation. You know that the substitution is the intended meaning, so the waiting is for the coming of the Hour suddenly, and the stated reason is a reason for the qualified element without its qualifier too. So what is in Irshad is the required reading, even though it contains some interpretation. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will they have their reminder when it comes to them?﴾ According to what some eminent scholars have stated, it is an expression of wonder at the benefit of the reminder at the time of the Hour's coming, and a denial of their lack of heed to it and their waiting for it in mockery and denial. In Irshad: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will they have their reminder when it comes to them?﴾ is a judgment of their error and the corruption of their opinion in delaying the reminder until its coming, by explaining the impossibility of the benefit of the reminder at that time, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ That is, how can they have their reminder? Furthermore, "how" (anna) is a predicate placed first, "their reminder" (dhikraahum) is the subject, and "when it comes to them" is a parenthetical clause placed between them, as a symbol of the extreme speed of its coming. The coming is stated without the qualifier of suddenness because the basis of the impossibility of the benefit of the reminder is that it is at the time of its coming absolutely, not restricted by the qualifier of suddenness. It was also said: "how" (anna) is a predicate placed first for an omitted subject, meaning: how will there be for them deliverance when the reminder comes to them, with what they report, which is connected to the punishment, and its state is not hidden.

Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, from the people of Makkah, read (in ta'tihim), as a conditional sentence newly begun whose apodosis is ﴿so how will they have...﴾ and so on. That is: if the Hour comes upon them suddenly, since its portents have already come, then how will the reminder benefit them at the time of its coming? "If" (in) here has the sense of "when" (idha), because the coming of the Hour is certain. Perhaps the use of the conditional here is to rebuke them and to show that they are in doubt about it, or because its time is not specified, it resembles what is doubtful. And when "when it comes to them" is taken in terms of the actual reality, there is no contradiction between them, as is imagined by the foolish glance.

In al-Kashf: "when" (idha) in this reading is merely for the sense of time, so that there is no conflict between "when it comes to them" and "if it comes to them." In the use of "that" (anna) together with certainty of occurrence there is a strengthening of the matter of rebuke and denial, as is not hidden. Ends. According to what we have mentioned, there is no need to make "when" merely for the sense of time.

Al-Ju'fi and Harun, from Abu Amr, read (baghatah) with a fatha on the ghayn and a shaddah on the ta'. The author of al-Lawami said: it is an adjective, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal). There is no parallel to it among verbal nouns or among adjectives, but rather among nouns, like jirbah, which is a herd of wild donkeys, and it is sometimes applied to strong people when they are a group of equals, jirbah; and shirbah, which is the name of a place. Abu al-Abbas ibn al-Hajj, one of the companions of Abu Ali al-Shalawbin, said the same in his book al-Masadir. Al-Zamakhshari said: how I fear that it is an error by the narrator from Abu Amr, and that the correct reading is (baghatan) with a fatha on the ghayn without shaddah, like the reading of al-Hasan mentioned earlier. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying that this is his habit of declaring narrators to be in error. The apparent meaning of "the portents of the Hour" here is its signs which were occurring at that time, and they reported that they were signs of it, like the sending of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'I was sent together with the Hour like these two,' and he pointed with the index and middle fingers." He, peace and blessings be upon him, intended to show the extreme nearness between his sending and the Hour, for the index finger is close to the middle finger in length on us, and likewise on him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Some claimed that the matter of length and shortness between his middle and index fingers, peace be upon him, is the opposite of what is with us, which is an error not to be heeded, unless he meant that regarding the toes of his blessed feet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Ahmad narrated from Buraydah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: 'I and the Hour were sent together, though it nearly outpaced me.'"

This is more emphatic in conveying nearness. They counted among its signs the splitting of the moon, which occurred for him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the smoke which occurred for the people of Makkah. As for its portents in general, they are many, and brief and lengthy books have been composed on them. They are divided into those that are restrictive, after whose occurrence the world will not remain except for a very little, such as the emergence of the Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, according to what the People of the Sunnah say, not what the Shi'ah say, who hold to the return (al-raj'ah), for according to them the world after his appearance remains for a considerable period; and the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, the emergence of the Dajjal, the rising of the sun from its west, the emergence of the beast, and other things. And those that are non-restrictive, which are the majority of the portents, such as the barefoot shepherds becoming the heads of people, their boasting in building, the spread of backbiting, the eating of usury, the drinking of wine, the exaltation of the owner of wealth, the scarcity of the noble and the abundance of the base, people boasting in mosques and making them thoroughfares, bad neighborliness, severing of kinship ties, the scarcity of knowledge, the matter being entrusted to other than its people, and the happiest of people in the world being the base son of a base father, and other things whose mention would be lengthy.

Whoever has looked into the books composed on this subject and has become acquainted with the conditions of the times sees that most of these signs have already appeared openly and that the regions have been filled with them. Despite all this, the matter of the Hour remains unknown, and the veil of concealment is drawn over it. The most that should be said is that what remains of the lifespan of the world is a very small amount compared to what has passed. In some reports: that he, peace and blessings be upon him, addressed his companions after the afternoon prayer, when the sun was about to set and only a little of it remained, and said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the likeness of what has passed of the world in what remains of it is only like what has passed of your day in what remains of it, and what remains of it is but little."

It should not be said that the second thousand after the Hijrah, which is the thousand we are in, is a mixed thousand, meaning half of it is from this world and half from the Hereafter. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti, in a treatise he named "al-Kashf 'an Mujawazah Hadhihi al-Ummah al-Alf" (The Disclosure Concerning This Nation Surpassing the Thousand), said: what the reports indicate is that the lifespan of this nation exceeds a thousand years, but the excess does not reach a thousand years. He built the matter on what has been transmitted, that the lifespan of the world is seven thousand years, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was sent at the end of the sixth thousand, that the Dajjal emerges at the head of a hundred, that Jesus, peace be upon him, descends and kills him, then remains on earth for forty years, that people remain after the rising of the sun from its west for a hundred and twenty years, and that between the two blasts is forty years. He mentioned the hadiths and reports concerning this.

In Bahjat al-Nazirin wa-Ayat al-Mustadillin: many scholars have argued for determining the nearness of its time by hadiths that are not free from scrutiny. Some of them said: "so-and-so remains," and others said: "the Dajjal will emerge at such-and-such a point, and the sun will rise at such-and-such a point." Al-Hafiz al-Suyuti devoted a treatise to all of that and said: "The Hour will take place around the year one thousand five hundred." All of that is rejected, and the speakers on this matter have only conjecture and supposition, for which no proof from revelation stands. End. Al-Safarini quoted it in al-Buhur al-Zakhirah fi Ulum al-Akhirah. Al-Suyuti also mentioned several reports about the world's lifespan being seven thousand years, the first of which is what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated in Nawadir al-Usul with his chain from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Intercession on the Day of Resurrection is only for those among my nation who committed major sins and died upon them; they are in the first gate of Hell.'" He continued the rest of the hadith, in which: "The one who remains longest in it is he who remains in it like the lifespan of the world since its creation until its destruction, and that is seven thousand years." The hadith.

Al-Safarini responded to it, saying: al-Hafiz Ibn Rajab mentioned in his book Sifat al-Nar that this hadith was narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim and others, and al-Isma'ili narrated it at length. Al-Daraqutni said in the book al-Mukhtalaf: "It is a munkar hadith," and he mentioned its defects. Among what al-Suyuti mentioned on this is what has been reported: the weakness of the chain of its raised form. It may be countered that from the time of the sending until our present day, one thousand two hundred and sixty-eight years have passed. If to this is added what he mentioned of the years of Jesus's stay, the remaining of the world after the rising of the sun from its west, and what is between the two blasts, which are two hundred years, it becomes one thousand four hundred and seventy-eight, and there remains from the period he mentioned twenty-two years. Until now the sun has not risen from its west, nor has the Dajjal emerged, whose emergence is some years before the rising of the sun from its west, nor has the Mahdi appeared, whose appearance is seven years before the Dajjal, nor have the portents which come before the appearance of the Mahdi occurred. It is hardly to be said that he will appear after fifteen years, and the Dajjal will appear seven years after that, at the head of the third century of the second thousand, because before that there are preliminaries which occur over many years. So the truth is that no one knows what remains of the lifespan of the world except Allah, mighty and majestic, and that however long it is, it is the shortest of the short, and "the enjoyment of the life of this world is but little." Likewise, in my view, the beginning of its creation is known only to Allah, exalted is He, and what they mention about the beginning, even if it is sound, refers only to the beginning of the creation of the successor Adam, peace be upon him, not the beginning of the creation of the heavens, the earth, the mountains and the like.

The Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may God sanctify his secret, related from Idris, peace be upon him, when he met him in a spiritual encounter, and asked him about the world. He said: "We, the company of the prophets, know that the world is originated (ḥādith), but we do not know when it originated." According to the well-known view, the philosophers claim that part of the world is eternal in its individual existence and part is eternal in its species, together with their saying that it is originated in its essence. They do not hold that it will perish.

Mulla Sadr al-Shirazi held that they affirm the eternity only of the immaterial intellects (al-ʿuqūl al-mujarrada), not of the world of bodies absolutely. Rather, they hold that bodies are originated and perishing. He extended his discussion of this in *al-Asfar* and cited the texts of their great figures, such as Aristotle and others.

Some of them relate that God created this world in which we live, the world of generation and corruption, and that its rising sign is Spica (al-Sunbula), and that it will perish after the passing of seventy-eight thousand years. That is when the period of rule of each of the twelve zodiacal signs (al-burūj) has passed and the matter reaches the sign of Libra (al-Mizan). They claim that the period of rule of Aries (al-Hamal) is twelve thousand years, and the period of rule of Taurus (al-Thawr) is a thousand years less, and so on down to Pisces (al-Ḥūt).

Al-Bakri related from Hermes (Hirmis) that he claimed that during the rule of Aries, Taurus and Gemini there was no animal on the earth. When the rule of Cancer came, the creatures of the water and the insects of the earth came into being. When the rule of Leo came, the four-footed creatures came into being. When the rule of Spica came, the first two humans, Adamanus and Hawanus, were born.

Some of them claimed that the duration of the world equals the time the fixed stars take to traverse the degrees of the celestial sphere, which are three hundred and sixty degrees. According to the view of many of them, traversing each degree takes one hundred years, so its duration is thirty-six thousand years. All of this is mere conjecture with no evidence for it.

Among the most astonishing things I have seen is what some Muslim scholars (al-Islamiyyin) have claimed: that the Hour will come after one thousand four hundred and seven years. They base this on God's saying: ﴿Do they await anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly?﴾ and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿It will not come to you except suddenly﴾, on the premise that the number of letters of *baghta* (suddenly) by the great reckoning (al-jummal al-kabir, the numerical value of the letters in the abjad system) is one thousand four hundred and seven. Someone might almost say that it is one thousand eight hundred and two, and that by counting the tāʾ marbūṭa (the feminine ending) it is four hundred, not five. For he saw some practitioners of numerology (ahl al-ḥisāb), as in the *Fatawa* of Khayr al-Din al-Ramli. Another may come and say that it is even more than that. He takes into account the expansion of the letters in the manner in which they said about the name Muhammad (ﷺ), that it contains the number of the messengers, peace be upon them. You know that such things are not becoming for any sensible person to rely upon or pay attention to. The firm and certain conviction is that none knows that except the Subtle, the All-Aware.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 19 (part 1 of 5):**

﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾ is consequent upon the whole story from the opening of the surah, not upon His saying, "Do they only await [the Hour]?" It is as if it were said: "When you know that the matter is as has been mentioned, namely the happiness of these and the wretchedness of those, then remain steadfast in what you are upon of knowledge of the Oneness (wahdaniyyah), for it is one of the requirements of happiness." The command was interpreted as a command to persist in the knowledge, because the Prophet's ﷺ knowledge of tawhid (Divine Unity) cannot be conditioned by the states that He, glorified is He, has mentioned. He (ﷺ) is one who affirms Divine Unity on the basis of knowledge of the state of what is revealed to him. Also, the meaning is: "hold fast to what you are in of the requirements of happiness, not to the pursuit of happiness." Some of the eminent scholars said: steadfastness is also attained by him (ﷺ), so his being commanded to it is a reminder to him of what Allah, exalted is He, has bestowed upon him, as a preparation for what follows. This was objected to on the ground that steadfastness means continuance, and it is with respect to future times. Although this must be attained by him (ﷺ) because of his being protected from error (ʿismah), the one who is protected is still commanded and forbidden, so he does what is commanded and abstains from what is forbidden, and this is necessary for ʿismah.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and believing women﴾, it has been said that it is also in the sense of steadfastness. The seeking of forgiveness is taken as a metaphor for what it entails of humility, self-abasement, and acknowledgment of shortcoming, because he (ﷺ) is either protected or forgiven, not persistent and heedless of seeking forgiveness. It has also been said: the verified view is that it is a preparation for what follows of seeking forgiveness for the believing men and believing women. Perhaps the better course is to keep it on its literal meaning without making it a preparation.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to frequently seek forgiveness. Aḥmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Hibban narrated from al-Aghurr al-Muzani, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, my heart is veiled, and I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times every day."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have never risen in the morning without seeking forgiveness from Allah a hundred times in it."

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and a group narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "We used to count for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in a single sitting, him saying: 'My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance, indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful,' a hundred times." In another wording: "the Accepting of repentance, the Forgiving." And there are other sound reports.

The sin with respect to him (ﷺ) is the abandoning of what is better for his lofty station. Many a thing that is a good deed from one person is a bad deed from another, as it is said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near." They have mentioned that our Prophet (ﷺ) has at every moment an ascent to a station higher than that in which he was, so what he ascends from is, in his noble view, a sin with respect to what he ascends to, and so he seeks forgiveness for it. They understood on this basis his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed, my heart is veiled..." and so on. There are other opinions regarding it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and for the believing men﴾ is by omission of a noun (muḍāf) indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "and for the sins of the believing men." The preposition is repeated because their sins are a different kind from his (ﷺ) sin, for their sins are acts of disobedience, both major and minor, while his (ﷺ) sin is the abandoning of what is better with respect to his lofty station. It is not far-fetched that it may be with respect to them, on account of their good deeds. It has been said: the omission of the noun and the linking of the seeking of forgiveness to their very selves indicates their extreme need for it, as if their selves were themselves sins; and similarly it indicates their great number. Some have permitted that the seeking of forgiveness for the believers means asking forgiveness for them and asking for its cause, such as commanding them to piety. In this there is a combination of the literal and the figurative, although its soundness is open to discussion. So the apparent meaning is to keep the word on its literal sense.

In placing the command to tawhid first is an indication of the great nobility of tawhid, for it is the foundation of the acts of obedience and the lamp of acts of worship. Concerning the "good word" (al-kalimah al-ṭayyibah) there are noble discussions and subtle refinements, and there is no harm in mentioning some of them, even though some of that has already preceded. So we say: The well-known view is that illa (إلا) is for exception. The noble name (Allah) is a substitute (badal) for the position of the subject of the negating lā (of genus). The predicate of lā is omitted. The substitution was objected to from two directions. The first: it is a substitution of part (badal baʿḍ), and there is no pronoun returning to the substituted element, which is a condition for it. It was answered by denying that it is a condition in every case, but rather it is a condition where partiality is not understood by a clue; here partiality is understood by the clue of the exception. The second: there is a contrast between the substituted element and the substitute, for the first is negated and the second affirmed.

al-Sirafi answered that it is a substitute for the first in its governance by the governing word, and that contrast in negation and affirmation does not prevent substitution, because the principle of the substitute is that the first is treated as if it had not been mentioned and the second is put in its place; the adjective and the noun it qualifies may likewise differ in this, as in "I passed by a man who is neither generous nor clever." Moreover, if it were said that the substitute in the exception is a distinct category, separate from other kinds of substitution, that would have a basis.

The problem concerning the predicate was raised: if it is estimated as "possible" (mumkin), it entails denying actual existence to the One, the true One, exalted is His majesty; if it is estimated as "existent" (mawjud), it entails not declaring Him free from the possibility of partnership; and to estimate a specific appropriate predicate for which there is no clue is also problematic. It has been said that because of the difficulty of this objection, the author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) and his followers went to the view that the statement needs no predicate at all. They made "illa Allah" the subject and "la ilaha" its predicate, the original being "Allah is a god," meaning worshipped in truth. But when it was intended to restrict the attribute to the one qualified, the predicate was placed first, and the subject was joined to illa, since the restricted element is what follows illa, and the intended element is what falls within the context of negation; and when the subject is joined to illa, its predicate must be placed first. It was objected that, apart from its artificiality, this entails constructing the predicate with lā, and lā constructs only the subject with it; moreover, if the matter were so, there would be no basis for the accusative of the noun following it, although a group has permitted it.

Some of the eminent scholars said: "There is no god but Allah," according to this view, is a proposition with both terms modified (maʿdulat al-ṭarafayn), like "the non-living is not knowing" in the sense of "the living is knowing." This does not remove the objection, as is clear. Others said: the predicate is "illa Allah," meaning "illa" together with the noble name. It was objected that the genus is different from each of its individuals, so how can the denial of the individual's difference from it be true? It was answered: unless it is said that this is based on the implication of the meaning of "min" (from), and what is understood is that from this genus there has been removed other than this individual. The better statement, as is said, is that the difference that is negated is difference in existence, not difference in concept, so that it is not refuted. There is no doubt that what is meant by the genus negated by lā here is the concept without consideration of its being realized in the individuals, all or some of them; so it is predicated, not in the sense of considering its non-realization in them at all, for it does not follow from not considering something that its non-existence is considered. When the predication is realized, the non-difference in existence is realized. So reflect on it.

Some said: lā has no predicate at all, according to what the Banu Tamim said about it. It was objected that then the statement would lack a judgment and a contract, which is false by consensus, since tawhid necessarily entails that. It is not far-fetched to say that the view that lā needs no predicate does not remove the compound of it and its noun from being a contract, because the meaning of the compound, such as "lā rajul" (there is no man), under this estimation, is the negation of this genus; so when we say "lā rajul illa Hatim," its meaning is that this genus is negated in other than this individual. It is marred, however, by the fact that composing speech from a particle and a noun is not a thing that has a way to it. It may be answered by what was said regarding the vocative, such as "Yā Zayd," that it stands in place of "ud'ūhu" (call him). The noble scholar, may his secret be sanctified, stated, in explaining what was transmitted from the Banu Tamim about the non-affirmation of a predicate for lā, that it may be based on the understanding that the meaning of the composition, as mentioned just now, is the negation of this genus. Then the word "illa" on this estimation means "other than" (ghayr), and there is no room for it to be for exception, not because of the apparent contradiction based on the idea that negating a genus of each individual contradicts affirming it for one of its individuals; this is answered by something like what Najm al-A'immah chose in resolving the apparent contradiction in such a phrase as "the people stood except Zayd," because the people negated from the action include Zayd, who is affirmed to have it, in what is understood: the genus excluded from this individual is negated within everything other than him. Nor is it because of what may be imagined, that the negated genus does not include what follows illa, which is the condition of the exception, for you have learned the difference between the genus without consideration of its realization in the individuals and the genus with consideration of its non-realization in them. Rather, if it were for exception, the statement would not yield tawhid, for its resulting meaning would be that this genus, on the supposition that this individual is not included in it, is negated; thus it is understood that it is not negated in individuals other than this individual, so where is tawhid? Therefore it is necessary to take it in the sense of "other than" (ghayr) and to make it follow the position of the subject of lā, either as a substitute for it or as a qualifier, as in the verse:

*"And every brother is parted from by his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan [stars]."*

So I saw it thus in some old manuscripts, and one of the teachers of our teachers, the scholar al-Tabaqjali, mentioned it in his treatise explaining the good word, and did not add any comment on it. In my view, what has been said against the view that illa is for exception on that estimation is not free from consideration. Then it has been said: when the content of the compound on that estimation is that this genus is negated in what is other than this individual, the proposition is personal (shakhṣiyyah), and it has a necessary consequence which is a universal proposition, namely our saying: "Every thing that is considered an individual of it other than this individual is negated." There is no improbability in any of that.

Many have gone to estimating the predicate as "existent" (mawjud), and answered the objection by saying that it entails denying the general possibility from the side of existence concerning the gods other than Allah, exalted is He. This is based on a definitive premise known to the intelligent: that the one worshipped in truth is none other than one whose existence is necessary (wajib al-wujud). The meaning therefore becomes: "There is no worshipped one in truth existent except Allah." And if he is not existent, he is not possible, for if he were possible, he would be necessary on the basis of the definitive premise, and so he would be existent. The good word has indicated that he is not existent, so he is not possible, because the negation of the consequent indicates the negation of the antecedent.

It was objected that although the definitive premise is correct in reality, it is not granted by the polytheists, for they worship idols and believe them to be gods, while acknowledging that they are possible and in need of a Creator. ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, "Allah."﴾ So a responsible person may affirm the good word and believe that the negation of existence does not entail the negation of possibility; thus, in his view, the existence of gods other than Allah, exalted is He, is possible, and so the utterance of the word would not be an explicit proof of his faith. And if the aforementioned premise were granted by all, it would be possible from the outset to estimate the predicate as "existent in essence" (mawjud bi-l-dhat), meaning: "There is no god existent in essence except Allah." And if other than Him, exalted is He, is not existent in essence, he is not deserving of worship, because what deserves it is none other than one necessary in essence.
