Two further answers have been established.

The first: "There is no god existing" (*lā ilāha mawjūd*) is a categorical negative proposition (*qaḍiyya sālibah ḥamliyyah*), which must have a modality, namely general possibility (*al-imkān al-ʿāmm*). The meaning is that the opposite side of the negation, which is the affirmation of existence, is not necessary for any deity except God, Exalted is He. He exists by general possibility; that is, the side of negation is not necessary for Him, Exalted is He. Therefore existence is necessary for Him, glorified is He, in order to realize the contradiction between the exception and the excepted.

The second: "There is no god existing by general possibility" is a universal negative proposition, possible and general. What results from the exception, which is its contradictory, is a particular affirmative proposition that is necessary: that is, "God exists by necessity."

It has been objected to both formulations that they hold only if each of the two parts, the exception and the excepted, is an independent proposition, and this is not accepted. The correct view among the grammarians (*ahl al-ʿarabiyyah*) is that they form a single statement restricted by the exception, so the rules of contradiction do not apply to them, unless it is interpreted in the linguistic sense. Also, making God "existing by necessity" a particular proposition involves laxity.

It was said: "It is possible to say that the implied predicate is 'existent' absolutely, whether actually or by possibility, using a term in both of its meanings, or by interpreting it as that to which the name 'existent' applies." This, as you see, is [weak]. It was also said: "It is permissible to estimate it as *mumkin* (possible)." Negating possibility entails negating existence, because the deity is necessarily existent (*wājib al-wujūd*), and the possibility of a thing's being characterized by necessary existence entails its being characterized by actual existence by necessity. So when possibility is derived from the good word (*al-kalimah al-ṭayyibah*), existence is also derived from it, since whatever is not existent is impossible to be necessarily existent. What is in this [view] of what has passed is known, so do not be heedless.

Some said: "The implied predicate is 'deserving of worship' (*mustaḥiqq lil-ʿibādah*). The meaning is: there is no god deserving of worship except God." There is no problem with this.

It was objected: "This is a specific predicate (*kawn khāṣṣ*), and its deletion requires an indicator (*qarīnah*), and there is no indicator, so the deletion is not valid." It was answered: "The indicator is like a fire on a mountain (*ka-nār ʿalā ʿalam*), because 'god' (*ilāh*) means 'the one worshipped,' so it indicates worship and its being deserved." This is supported by observing the context and considering the condition of the addressees, because this good word came to refute the belief of the polytheists who claimed that idols deserve worship.

It was also objected: "It does not indicate the negation of plurality absolutely, that is, neither by possibility nor by actuality, since there may exist another god, glorified is He, who does not deserve worship." Furthermore, it can be said: "The intended meaning is either the negation of a god deserving worship other than Him, Exalted is He, in actuality or by possibility. On the first [meaning], it does not negate the possibility of another god deserving worship, other than Him, mighty and majestic. On the second, it does not indicate that He deserves worship in actuality." It was answered: "Necessary existence is the source of all perfections, and for this reason many of them have been derived from it. There is no doubt that it entails deserving exaltation and veneration, and there is no meaning to deserving worship except that. So if no one other than Him, Exalted is He, deserves worship, then no other being with necessary existence exists, otherwise it would certainly deserve worship. And if it does not exist, it is not possible either. Thus it is established that negating the deserving of worship entails negating plurality, with certainty."

It was criticized: "This involves building on the premise that a god is only necessarily existent, and you have heard that although the statement is definitively true in itself, it is not accepted by the polytheists." Some scholars of verification (*al-muḥaqqiqīn*) said: "No attention is given to their non-acceptance, because of their obstinacy about what might be self-evident." Yes, it may be said that the good word on that estimation indicates only the negation of an actually worshipped object, based on what has been established in logic (*al-manṭiq*) that the subject itself must actually be characterized by the title. It is answered: "There is no necessity for that; rather, characterization by possibility suffices, as al-Farabi (*al-Fārābī*) explicitly stated. As for what was transmitted from the Shaykh, its meaning is that it is actual according to the rational supposition, not according to the reality itself, as his expression in *al-Shifā'* and *al-Ishārāt* indicates; so it returns to the meaning of possibility."

The difference between the two positions is that in the Shaykh's position there is an additional consideration not found in al-Farabi's: the Shaykh took into account, alongside possibility, the supposition of actual characterization according to the reality itself, which al-Farabi did not consider. In sum, actual characterization is not necessary; so whatever can be characterized by worship-worthiness falls under the ruling that it does not deserve worship. And since the proposition is negative, it is true even if the subject does not exist. Perhaps the verification in this matter is that the good word circulates among people according to the common understanding of language and custom, not according to the logical technical terms and philosophical refinements. It is a statement that came to refute the belief of the polytheist who believed that gods other than God, glorified is He, deserve worship. So when the polytheist acknowledges its content, that there is no worshipped object deserving worship except God, Exalted is He, faith is known from the apparent condition of his state, and for this reason the Lawgiver (*al-Shāriʿ*), upon him be blessings and peace, was satisfied with it. As for the disbeliever who believes it is possible that a being deserving worship will exist afterward, this good word does not suffice for his faith, just as it does not suffice for the faith of one who denies prophethood, the Hereafter, or the like of what must be believed; rather, he must acknowledge the ruling he denied. There is no problem with this. And since the disbelievers who believe that gods other than God, Exalted is He, deserve worship are the well-known ones, rather than those who believe in the possibility of their existence afterward, the statement is considered a proper name (*ʿalam*) for monotheism (*tawḥīd*) with respect to them.

From this it is known that if the omitted predicate is estimated from the outset as "existent" (*mawjūd*), the difficulty can be removed by this way, namely the common understanding of language and the custom of ordinary people. As for the claim that negating existence does not entail negating possibility, the good word then does not entail negating the possibility of gods other than God, Exalted is He. This does not occur to minds, and hardly any disbeliever is found who believes in the negation of the existence of another god, Exalted is He, while believing in the possibility of the existence of another god, glorified is He, after that.

Some people supported the estimation of the predicate in that way, saying: "The apparent [meaning] is that *lā* is negating the genus (*nāfiyah lil-jins*), and negating the quiddity itself without considering existence and its characterization by it is like negating blackness itself, not negating its existence from it. It is far-fetched." Just as making a thing [exist] by considering existence, since there is no meaning to making a thing and rendering it itself, likewise negating and removing it [considers] also the removal of existence from it. It was criticized: "This is what the noble consideration (*al-naẓar al-jalīl*) requires, but the subtle consideration (*al-naẓar al-daqīq*) may judge otherwise, because negating a quiddity by considering existence ultimately ends in negating the quiddity of something by considering itself. This is because negating its characterization by existence does not happen by considering that characterization's own characterization by it, ad infinitum. So there must be an end to an attribute negated in itself, not by considering its characterization by existence, in order to avoid infinite regress (*tasalsul*)." It was said: "The apparent [meaning] is that the negation of entities, as in the good word, is only by considering that, whereas for other [statements] it varies. So reflect."

As for *illā* (except), on the stated estimation it is for exception, and the raising of the glorious name (*al-ism al-jalīl*) is as you have heard from the well-known view. It was said: "It is, in this [statement], in the sense of *ghayr* (other than), a qualifier of the noun, not according to the place of the word (*lā bi-iʿtibār al-maḥall*), meaning: there is no god other than God, Exalted is He, existing." It was objected: "The intended meaning of the statement is two matters: negating divinity from other than Him, Exalted is He, and affirming it for Him, glorified is He. This is complete only if *lā* is with *illā* for exception, since then negation and affirmation are derived by the explicit meaning (*manṭūq*). But if *illā* is in the sense of *ghayr*, it indicates by its explicit meaning only the negation of divinity from other than Him, Exalted is He. And whether affirming it for Him, Exalted is He, is by implication (*mafhūm*), and whether it suffices, is a matter of investigation. For if that is the implication of a title (*mafhūm laqab*), it has no weight according to those who accept implication, by the correct view, unlike al-Daqqaq and al-Sayrafi of the Shafi'is, Ibn Khuwayz Mindad of the Malikis, and Mansur ibn Ahmad of the Hanbalis. And if it is the implication of a qualifier (*mafhūm ṣifah*), then it is clearly not agreed upon, rather Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, did not say anything of the implications of opposition at all."

You know that what he mentioned, that the good word indicates the affirmation of divinity for God, Exalted is He, and its negation from other than Him, mighty and majestic, on the supposition that *illā* is for exception, is also not agreed upon, for the exception from a negation is not an affirmation according to Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him. Making affirmation in the statement of monotheism is by the usage of the Lawgiver (*bi-ʿurf al-shar'*), and in the incomplete construction (*al-mufarragh*), such as *mā qāma illā Zayd* (no one stood except Zayd), it is by general usage. What is for and against it in the books of legal theory (*kutub al-uṣūl*) is [known], so do not be heedless.

The complete discussion concerning the grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) of this good word is in the books of Arabic grammar. We have mentioned that in our notes on al-Suyuti's commentary on the *Alfiyyah*. According to the Sufi masters, may their secrets be sanctified, it comprises all levels of monotheism (*tawḥīd*) and indicates them, either explicitly or by implication. Its levels are four:

The first: the monotheism of divinity (*tawḥīd al-ulūhiyyah*).
The second: the monotheism of acts (*tawḥīd al-afʿāl*).
The third: the monotheism of attributes (*tawḥīd al-ṣifāt*); or, if you wish, you may say: the monotheism of essential necessary existence (*tawḥīd al-wujūb al-dhātī*), for it entails all the perfect attributes, as some verifiers derived them from it.
The fourth: the monotheism of essence (*tawḥīd al-dhāt*); or, if you wish, you may say: the monotheism of true existence (*tawḥīd al-wujūd al-ḥaqīqī*), for the end result is one according to them.

The explanation of this is that "There is no god but God" (*lā ilāha illā Allāh*), its explicit meaning, according to what comes first to minds and what the majority adopted, is the restriction of divinity to God, Exalted is He, by true restriction (*qaṣr ḥaqīqī*), that is, affirming it for Him, Exalted is He, by necessity, and negating it from everything other than Him, glorified is He, likewise. This entails the monotheism of acts, the monotheism of attributes, and the monotheism of essence.

As for the first, which is the restriction of creatorship to Him, Exalted is He: the requirement of restricting divinity to Him, Exalted is He, by true restriction, is that God, mighty and majestic, is the One whom every creature deserves to worship. He is the Benefiter, the Harmer, absolutely. He, glorified and exalted is He, is the Creator of everything, for whoever is not the Creator of everything is not an absolute Benefiter or Harmer, and whoever is not like that does not deserve that every creature worship him, since worship is obedience, submission, and humility. Whoever does not possess benefit or harm with respect to some creatures does not deserve that those creatures worship him, obey him, and submit to him, for whoever cannot bring benefit to a person or repel harm from him is not hoped in by him, and whoever cannot bring harm to him is not feared by him, and whoever is not feared or hoped in at all does not deserve to be worshipped. This is evident. But what the restriction of divinity to Him, Exalted is He, by true restriction requires is that God, Exalted is He, is the One whom every creature deserves to worship, He being the Benefiter, the Harmer.

[Page 59]

On an absolute basis, He is the Creator of everything, and He is the one sought. As for the second point, the good word (al-kalimah al-tayyibah) indicates that divinity (al-uluhiyyah) is established for Him, Exalted is He, with a continuous establishment that cannot be severed, and that divinity is negated from anyone else with a similar negation. Whatever is like this indicates that He, Mighty and Majestic, is necessarily existent (wajib al-wujud, the one whose existence is necessary in itself), and that every existent other than Him, Exalted is He, is possibly existent (mumkin al-wujud, whose existence is contingent). Whatever is like this means that necessary existence is restricted to Him, Exalted is He, and this implies all the attributes of perfection, which is the point to be proven.

As for its indication that He, Mighty and Majestic, is necessarily existent: divinity can belong only to something that truly exists, by consensus. Whatever cannot be an attribute except of an existent thing, if a statement indicates that it is established for a thing with an establishment that cannot be severed, eternally, then it indicates that existence is established for that thing with an establishment that cannot be severed, eternally. This is not so unless that thing exists in itself, and this is what is meant by necessary existence in itself. Since it indicates the establishment of divinity with a continuous establishment that cannot be severed, it indicates the necessity of His existence, Exalted is He, and this implies all the attributes of perfection, which is the point to be proven.

As for its indication that every existent other than Him is possibly existent: if any existent other than Him were necessarily existent in itself, it would deserve to be worshipped. But the good word has indicated that none deserves to be worshipped except Allah. Therefore it has indicated that nothing whose existence is necessary in itself exists except Allah, Exalted is He, and so everything else is possibly existent, which is the point to be proven. Or it may be said: it has indicated that He, Exalted is He, is the One who benefits and harms in the absolute sense, and so He is the one who combines the attributes of majesty and generosity. He, Glorified is He, is characterized by all the attributes of perfection, which is the point to be proven.

As for the third point: Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali) said in the chapter on truthfulness in the Ihya' (Revival of the Religious Sciences): Whatever a servant is bound to is his slave, as 'Isa, peace be upon him, said: "O slaves of this world." And our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "(Wretched is the slave of the dinar, wretched is the slave of the dirham, and the slave of the fine garment, and the slave of the cloak.)" Everyone whose heart is bound to something is called its slave. He also said in the chapter on asceticism in the same work: Whoever seeks other than Allah, Exalted is He, has worshipped it, and everything sought is worshipped, and every seeker is a slave in relation to what he seeks. He said in the third chapter of the Book of Knowledge from the same work: Every follower of his desire has taken his desire as a god. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you seen one who has taken his desire as his god?﴾ [45:23]. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "The most hateful god worshipped on earth in the sight of Allah, Exalted is He, is desire." End of quotation.

It is known that nothing in existence exists except that it is sought by some seeker. It has been established by what preceded that the term "god" (ilah) applies to it, and "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). Therefore nothing in existence is a true reality except Allah. Some scholars have established the indication of the good word on the oneness of the Essence and the negation of the existence of anyone other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, by another way: that "illa" (except) in the sense of "ghayr" (other than) is a substitute (badal) for the negated "ilah," so the negation is in reality directed at the other, and the negation of the other is, in their view, true monotheism (tawhid haqiqi). When its indication of all stages of monotheism has become clear to you, it becomes evident that the Lawgiver made it, for a reason, the key to Islam, the foundation of the religion, and the guidance gift of mankind.

In a hadith narrated by Abu Nu'aym from 'Iyad al-Ash'ari, that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "(There is no god but Allah is a noble word, and it has a place with Allah. It has gathered and it has been made complete. Whoever says it sincerely from his heart enters Paradise.)"

In a hadith narrated by Ibn al-Najjar from Dinar, from Anas, that he, peace be upon him, said: "(There is no god but Allah is a great and noble word with Allah, Exalted is He. Whoever says it sincerely deserves Paradise.)"

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Go with these my two sandals, and whoever you meet behind this wall bearing witness that there is no god but Allah, with certainty in his heart, give him the good news of Paradise."

The hadith of the card (al-bitaqah) is too well known to be mentioned. Likewise the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi) narrated from 'Ali al-Rida from his fathers, peace be upon them. And there has come: "(Whoever's last words in this world are: There is no god but Allah, enters Paradise.)"

That is, without reckoning; otherwise, what is the difference between that and one who says it but it is not his last words in this world? In sum, its virtue cannot be counted, and it leads its sayer to the highest station. Books have been composed on its virtue, the manner of pronouncing it, and the etiquette of using it, so we will not prolong the discussion of that.

There remains here a question: the Muslims have agreed on the obligation of knowing Allah, Exalted is He, although they differ over whether this obligation is revealed (shar'i) or rational ('aqli). As for reflection (nazar) in order to attain knowledge of Him, Exalted is He, to the extent of human capacity, the Allamah al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Maqasid: There is no disagreement among the people of Islam about its obligation, because it is a matter within one's power, upon which the absolutely obligatory depends, namely knowledge, and everything within one's power upon which the absolutely obligatory depends is obligatory, by revelation if the obligation of the absolutely obligatory is revealed, as is the view of the Ash'ari scholars, or by reason if it is rational, as is the view of the Mu'tazilah, so as to avoid imposing the impossible. As for reflection being within one's power, this is evident. As for knowledge depending on it, this is because knowledge is not self-evident but acquired, and an acquired thing means only that which depends on reflection and is obtained through it. The apparent words of al-Sanad in his commentary on al-Mawaqif indicate consensus of all Muslims on this as well. The truth is that disagreement has occurred over the obligation of reflection, as indicated by the words of Ibn al-Hajib in his Mukhtasar, al-'Adud in his commentary, the words of Taj al-Din al-Subki in Jam' al-Jawami', al-Jalal al-Mahalli in his commentary, and the statement of Shaykh al-Islam in his gloss on it: the place of disagreement is the obligation of reflection in the foundations of religion, and its non-obligation regarding other than knowing Allah, Exalted is He, from among them. As for reflection on them, it is obligatory by consensus, as al-Sa'd al-Taftazani and others mentioned. The verifier Ibn Qasim al-'Abbadi objected to this in his gloss, al-Ayat al-Bayyinat, saying: It is evident that what al-Sa'd transmitted as consensus on the obligation of reflection on knowing Allah, Exalted is He, is not accepted by the commentator and others. Do you not see the commentator's example of the place of disagreement, saying: such as the origination of the world, the existence of the Creator, Exalted is He, and what is necessary for Him, Glorified is He, and what is impossible for Him, Glorified is He, of attributes? For his words "and the existence of the Creator, Exalted is He, etc." relate to knowledge of Him, Mighty and Majestic, to the end of what he said. Yes, many scholars said, and al-Imam al-Razi and al-Amidi preferred, that reflection is obligatory in matters of belief, and knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, is their foundation, so it is obligatory in them with greater priority. They said this because the aim is certainty, based on His saying, Exalted is He, to His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾ [47:19], and he already knew it. He, Exalted is He, said to people: ﴿And follow him that you may be guided﴾ [7:158]. Other than the oneness is analogized to it, and the argument is not complete unless one adds that attaining certainty depends on reflection. These scholars did not permit taqlid (imitation) in the foundations, and this is one of the views on the question. The second view is that of al-'Anbari: taqlid is permissible in them with firm conviction, and reflection on them is not obligatory, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to be satisfied with firm conviction in faith, and other than faith is analogized to it.

What is meant is that he, peace be upon him, was satisfied with that, considering the apparent state, for the report, as the verifier 'Isa al-Safawi clearly stated in his commentary on al-Fawa'id al-Ghiyathiyyah, as transmitted from him by his student Ibn Qasim al-'Abbadi in al-Ayat al-Bayyinat, indicates by convention a mental image in the manner of assent that reflects the actual state. There is no doubt that "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" belongs to the category of report, so both indicate by convention that their sayer, even under the shadow of the sword, holds their content with assent. That he does not hold it in reality is a rational possibility, and the One who knows what is in hearts is the Knower of the unseen. The third view is that taqlid with firm conviction is obligatory, and reflection is stirred up, because it is a likely cause of falling into doubts and misguidance due to the differences of minds, unlike taqlid. This is not a valid view at all. As for those verifiers who made reflection obligatory, they did not mean reflection in the manner of the theologians (mutakallimun), but rather, as stated in al-Jawab al-'Atid by al-Kurani, that the required reflection is that of the common people. Apparently it is not a likely cause of falling into what was mentioned. Whether those who hold it obligatory make it a condition for the validity of faith or not is a matter of dispute. From some expressions of the commentary on al-Arba'in by Ibn Hajar it is understood that he makes it a condition, so the faith of the imitator is not valid according to him. Rather, from them it is understood that the reflection required in that case is reflection in the manner of the theologians. The words of al-Jalal al-Mahalli in his commentary on Jam' al-Jawami' are explicit that the advocates of the obligation of reflection, other than Abu Hashim, do not make reflection a condition for the validity of faith, nor do they claim the invalidity of the faith of the imitator; rather it is valid in their view along with sin for leaving the obligatory reflection. Yes, it will come, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills, that the Imam Hujjat al-Islam, in his book Fayṣal al-Tafriqah bayn al-Islam wa al-Zandaqah, transmits the stipulation from a group of theologians along with his refutation of it.

As for what is transmitted from Shaykh al-Ash'ari regarding the stipulation, and that the faith of the imitator is not valid, it is a lie against him, as Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri stated. Taj al-Din al-Subki said: The verified position is that if taqlid is accepting another's word without evidence, with a possibility of doubt or illusion, then it does not suffice; but if it is certainty, then it suffices, contrary to Abu Hashim. Apparently, the one who holds that taqlid with certainty suffices rejects the claim that knowledge is attained only through reflection, and says: it may be attained through inspiration, instruction, or purification. So whoever attains firm conviction in what he is obliged to believe, his faith is valid without sin, because the aim has been achieved. And whoever does not attain that, either initially, or by taqlid, or by necessity, then reflection is required of him. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them?﴾ [18:57].
