Sufficient as evidence for the soundness of this view is the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) accepted from the common folk of the non-Arabs, and from the rough Arab nomads, those who embraced Islam under the shadow of the sword merely by affirming "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Their outward state indicated that they believed what this entailed and submitted to it. Had reflection (*istidlal*) been obligatory, they would have been commanded to undertake it after pronouncing the two testimonies, or they would have been taught the proof and instructed in it just as they were taught the two testimonies and as they were taught all other obligations. Had this occurred, it would have been transmitted to us, for it is among the most important matters of the religion. No report has come down that they ordered any of those who embraced Islam to undertake reflection, nor that they asked them about the proof for their assent, nor that they deferred their affair until they had reflected. If reflection were obligatory upon every individual, even in a general (*ijmali*) manner in the way of the common people, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have been satisfied from those common folk and rough nomads with the mere affirmation, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions do not permit anyone to abandon an individual obligation (*fard al-ayn*) without excuse. Thus the one who abandons it would not be sinful, let alone be one whose faith is invalid because of that abandonment.

This is supported by what the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Usama ibn Zayd when he offered an excuse for killing Mirdas ibn Nahik of the people of Fadak, as well as by many other reports.

As for what is stated in *al-Mawaqif*, *al-Maqasid*, the commentary on *al-Mukhtasar* by al-Adudi (*Sharh al-Mukhtasar al-'Adudi*), and other books of theology (*kalam*) and principles of jurisprudence (*usul*), namely that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions knew that the common people and the rough Arab nomads know the proofs in a general way, as the Bedouin said: "The camel dung indicates the camel, and the track of footprints indicates the traveller. Does the sky with its constellations and the earth with its paths not indicate the All-Subtle, the All-Aware?"—the meaning is that for this reason they did not oblige them to reflect, nor did they ask them about it, nor did they defer their affair. Whatever is of this kind, their being satisfied with the mere affirmation is not evidence that reflection is not obligatory upon every individual, nor evidence that the one who abandons it is not sinful. This is an assertion for which there is no evidence.

Moreover, if the Bedouin's saying is cited as an argument, it proves at most that this Bedouin possessed knowledge of a general proof. It does not follow from this that all the rough folk and common people possessed knowledge of general proofs in the time of prophethood or at other times; otherwise it would be a proof that there is no imitator (*muqallid*) in existence. Furthermore, some have attributed that saying to Qass ibn Sa'ida, who lived in the period between prophets (*al-fatra*). Al-Jalal al-Mahalli (*al-Jalal al-Mahalli*) mentioned it as the saying of a Bedouin in reply to al-Asma'i, who lived in the time of al-Rashid.

Indeed, it may be said that the apparent meaning of many verses and reports indicates that many of the polytheists in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) did not know the proofs of monotheism (*tawhid*) at all. This is like the saying of Allah, related about them:

*[Page 63 continues]*

﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾

﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," they were arrogant. And they said, "Shall we abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾

And the saying of one of them in one of the battles: "Exalt Hubal! Exalt Hubal!"

As for what the verifier (*al-muhaqqiq*) al-Adud mentioned in the commentary on *al-Mukhtasar* as evidence for the impermissibility of imitation (*taqlid*), where he said: The community is unanimous that knowledge of Allah the Exalted is obligatory, and that it is not attained through imitation, for three reasons:

First: It is possible that the informant lies, so knowledge is not attained by his statement.

Second: If it did yield knowledge, it would yield it concerning issues of dispute such as the createdness of the world. Then if one person imitates in the view of its being created and another in the view of its being eternal, both would be knowers of both opposites, which entails the joining of contradictories, and that is impossible.

Third: If imitation were to yield knowledge, then the knowledge that he spoke truly in what he reported is either necessary (*darury*) or acquired by reasoning (*nazari*). It cannot be the latter, so it must be the former. But necessary knowledge requires a proof, and it is assumed that there is no proof; for if its truth were known through its proof, it would no longer be imitation.

Al-Allama al-Kurani (*al-'Allama al-Kurani*) critiqued this, saying: In it there is discussion. As for the first reason, the one who permits imitation is like the imitator who grew up on the peak of a mountain, did not reflect on the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and was told by another what he must believe; he believes it and accepts its truth simply by being told, without contemplation or reflection. This is explicit that the discussion concerns an imitator who was told by another what he must believe, and what he must believe can only be true, for no one is obliged to believe a lie. As for one who reports falsehoods and believes them, he believes nothing but falsehoods, and falsehoods are not part of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted at all. How then could any sensible person judge of him that he is a believer in Allah the Exalted and a knower of Him, when he believes nothing but falsehoods? This is evident.

As for the second reason, it is for the same reason as above: we do not say that every imitation yields knowledge, nor that every imitator is a knower. How could we, when not every reflection yields knowledge, nor does every reflector attain the truth? Since reflection does not necessarily yield knowledge absolutely, but only correct reflection does, likewise we say: not every imitation yields knowledge, but only correct imitation does. This is when one imitates a scholar of the issues of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted who speaks truly in what he tells him. The discussion concerns the soundness of the faith of such an imitator, not imitation in general.

As for the third reason, we choose that his knowledge that he spoke truly in what he reported is necessary. Your statement that there is no way to it by necessity we deny, on the basis of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam.﴾

It has been transmitted as a raised report (*marfu'*) that he (ﷺ) was asked about the expansion of the breast, and he said (ﷺ): "It is a light which Allah casts into the heart of the believer, and it expands." So he (ﷺ) explicitly stated that it is a light which is not obtained from a proof, but which Allah casts into his heart, so he cannot repel it without thought, deliberation, reflection, or reasoning. Some of the great verifiers have stated that the monotheism of the prophets (peace be upon them) was from necessary knowledge they found in their souls, which they could not repel; and that among the people of the interval (*ahl al-fatra*) there were those who found it likewise. Indeed, he has stated that faith is a necessary knowledge which the believer finds in his heart and cannot repel. How many have believed without proof, and how many have not believed despite proof! And rarely is the faith of one who believed through proof trusted, for he is exposed to corrupting doubts.

In the chapter 172, the chapter 177, and the chapter 277 of *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya* (*al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*) there is something that confirms this.

Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali) said in *Fasl al-Tafriqa* (*Fasl al-Tafriqa*): Among the people most extreme and deviant are a group of theologians who declared the common Muslims to be unbelievers and claimed that whoever does not know theology as we know it, and does not know the legal proofs through our proofs which we have established, is an unbeliever. These people first narrowed the vast mercy of Allah upon His servants, and made Paradise a preserve of a small handful of theologians. Then secondly they ignored what the Sunna had transmitted through continuous narration (*tawatur*), for it is manifest from the era of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the era of the Companions (may Allah's good pleasure be upon them all) that they judged as Muslims groups of rough Arab nomads who were occupied with idol worship, and who did not occupy themselves with teaching the proofs; and even if they had occupied themselves with them, they would not have understood them. Whoever thinks that the means of attaining faith is theology, the formulated proofs, and the ordered divisions has strayed far. Rather, faith is a light which Allah the Exalted casts into the heart of His servant, as a gift and guidance from Him: sometimes through an awakening in the inner self which cannot be expressed,

*[Page 64]*

and sometimes through a dream in sleep, and sometimes through witnessing the condition of a pious man and the spread of his light to him in his company and session, and sometimes through an indication of circumstance. A Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) denying him and rejecting him, but when his gaze fell upon his radiant countenance and the youthful brightness of his face overwhelmed him, and he saw the light of prophethood shining from it, he said: "By Allah, this is not the face of a liar." He asked him to present Islam to him, and he embraced Islam. Another came and said: "I beseech you by Allah, has Allah sent you as a prophet?" He (ﷺ) said: "Yes, by Allah, Allah has sent me as a prophet." He affirmed it with his right hand and embraced Islam. So this and its like are more than can be counted, and not one of them ever occupied himself with theology or learning the proofs. Rather, the lights of faith first appeared in their hearts through such indications as a white gleam, and then they never ceased to increase in clarity and radiance through witnessing those great states, through the recitation of the Qur'an, and through the purification of hearts.

I wish I knew who transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and from the Companions that they brought a Bedouin who had embraced Islam and made him state the proof that the world is created, because it does not escape accidents (*a'rad*), and whatever does not escape temporal events is itself temporal; and that Allah the Exalted is knowing by a knowledge and powerful by a power, both of which are additional to the essence, neither identical with it nor other than it; and so on through the other formulae of the theologians. I do not say that these expressions were not used; rather, I say that nothing whose meaning is the meaning of these expressions was used either. Rather, no battle was ever concluded except with a group of rough folk who embraced Islam under the shadows of swords, and a group of captives who embraced Islam one by one after a long time or soon after. And when they pronounced the testimony of faith, they were taught the prayer and the zakat, and were returned to their trades, such as tending sheep or other things.

Yes, I do not deny that the mention of the proofs of the theologians may be one of the causes of faith for some people. But that is not restricted to it, and it is also rare. He went on to say: The clear truth is that everyone who firmly believes that what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and what the Qur'an contains, is true, is a believer, even if he does not know its proofs. Faith borrowed from the theological proofs is very weak and very near to wavering at every doubt. Rather, firm faith is the faith of the common people which settles in their hearts in childhood through continuous hearing, and which is attained after puberty through circumstances for which no expression is possible. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 19 (part 5 of 5):

There are many benefits in this, which is why we have quoted it in full. If it is possible for Allah, exalted is He, to cast the light of faith into the heart of a servant, so that he believes without reflection or inference, then it is also possible for Him, glorified is He, to cast into his heart the truthfulness of the one who informs him, to the point that he cannot repel it and does not know where it came from. This is especially so when the one who informs is the Prophet (ﷺ). For it is necessary, when the light of faith is cast into the heart of a believer in him, peace and blessings be upon him, that the truthfulness of (the Prophet) (ﷺ) also be cast into his heart, because faith is not complete except with this. It has thus become clear that the claim of necessity (darura), that there is no way to attain knowledge of the truthfulness of the informant regarding what he reports except by necessary knowledge, if it is not wilful denial (mukabara), then rejecting it is not wilful denial either. For the proof has established the possibility of necessary knowledge of his truthfulness, indeed its actual occurrence. So that claim is not among the necessary premises whose rejection would be wilful denial and unacceptable.

It has also become clear from all that has been mentioned that what al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) stated in his commentary on al-Maqasid, namely that the truth is that knowledge through a general (ijmali) proof, which lifts the examiner from the depths of taqlid (blind adherence), is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) from which no one among the responsible persons (mukallafun) may be exempt, while knowledge through a detailed (tafsili) proof, by which one is able to remove doubts (shubah), refute deniers and guide seekers of guidance, is a collective obligation (fard kifaya) that some must undertake, is open to question, as has been said. Nevertheless, in my view the apparent position is that the truth lies with al-Sa'd, on the basis that faith in the sense of assent (tasdiq) is something one is obligated to, and a condition of what one is obligated to is that it be within one's power (ikhtiyari). They have stated explicitly that obligation to something not within one's power is in reality an obligation to what it depends upon of matters within one's power. And since assent itself is not within one's power, the obligation to it is in reality an obligation to what it depends upon, namely voluntary reflection (nazar ikhtiyari). Therefore, the faith that comes about through Allah, exalted is He, casting the light into the heart without thought, deliberation, reflection or inference is not within one's power in itself, nor in terms of what results from it. How then could one be obligated to it?

What al-Sa'd and those who agree with him mean by knowledge is only knowledge insofar as it is something one is obligated to, as his words indicate: "there is no escape from it for any of the responsible persons." That this is obligatory is by reason of a voluntary matter other than reflection, such as preparing oneself to receive the light. The creation of necessary knowledge in the heart of a servant is not evident.

Yes, I do not deny that there is knowledge that does not depend on reflection on a general proof or any other, such as the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them, as you have heard about some of them, and the knowledge of whomever Allah, exalted is He, wills among His other servants. I do not call such knowledge taqlidi (blind adherence). I also do not deny that the knowledge obtained from the casting of the light is superior to the knowledge obtained from reflection on the proof, for it is feared to be exposed to the storms of doubts. However, I hold that reflection on the proof in general is obligatory upon one who has not attained firm conviction except through it. As for one who has attained that conviction by any means other than it, it is not obligatory for him, and likewise he is not sinful for abandoning it. The report of consensus (ijma') on his sinfulness in doing so is not free from problems. The justification for this, that the conviction of the believer in that case is not reliable, since if a doubt arises he loses it and remains hesitant, unlike conviction arising from inference, which is not lost in this way, is not evident. For if it is granted that one whose conviction is complete without reflection has fulfilled the obligation of faith, there is no basis for sinning him for abandoning reflection on the basis of the mere possibility that a disturbing doubt might arise against his conviction. For if it is granted that the obligation upon him is only that he be convinced, and he is convinced, then he has discharged the obligation of the time and left nothing of it undone. Whoever has not abandoned a specific obligation at a specific time, there is no sense in sinning him at that time on account of that obligation. Just as it is rationally possible that a doubt might arise that disturbs his conviction because there is no proof, it is likewise rationally possible that he might obtain a proof for what he was convinced of before a doubt arose. Indeed, this possibility is stronger and closer to occurring.

When you have comprehended all that we have mentioned, you will know that the use of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾ as evidence for the obligation of reflection on it is problematic, since it depends on the soundness of their claim that knowledge is not attained except through reflection, and you have heard what is wrong with that. This is strengthened if we say that his knowledge (ﷺ) of the oneness (wahdaniyya) of Allah was necessary, for the intended meaning would then be the command to persist and continue in what he (ﷺ) was upon, namely avoiding what would undermine knowledge. It may be said, however, that the inference could be made by reference to the apparent wording, insofar as it is a command to know the oneness of Allah. So it must be something within one's power, either in itself or in terms of what results from it. Since it is not within one's power in itself, it is necessarily within one's power in terms of what results from it, and the apparent meaning is that this is reflection.

You know that if taqlid is also a cause among the causes of knowledge, then this does not hold. And if it is not a cause, then it holds. So consider this carefully.

Furthermore, know that the reflection that the scholars have spoken of regarding the principles of belief ('aqa'id) is more general than reflection on rational proofs and reflection on transmitted (sam'i) proofs. For among these are matters established by transmission, such as the matters of the Hereafter, and the role of reason in them is only that they are possible things which the Truthful One (al-Sadiq) has informed us will occur, and every possible thing which the Truthful One has informed us will occur does occur. Therefore those matters occur. As for reflection on knowing Allah, exalted is He, meaning assent to His existence and His exalted attributes, it has been said that the intended meaning must be reflection on rational proofs only, and it is not permissible that reflection on transmitted proofs be the path to it, since that would entail circular reasoning (dawr).

In the well-prepared reply, circular reasoning is indeed entailed, but not absolutely. Rather, it is entailed with respect to every matter on which the knowledge of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) depends upon knowledge of it. This is because reflection on transmitted proofs is only a path to knowledge when those proofs are considered true by the one reflecting on them. And their truth in the knower's knowledge depends on his knowing that this one who claims to be the Messenger of Allah, who brought them, is truthful in his claim to prophethood. And his knowledge of that depends on knowing that Allah, exalted is He, has manifested miracles at his hand as confirmation of his claim. And his knowledge of that depends on knowing that there is a god with an attribute by which He can send a messenger, such as being living, knowing, willing and powerful, which is part of the knowledge of the Divine, glorified is He. So if we were to derive knowledge of the existence of Allah, exalted is He, and of those attributes from transmitted proofs, which depend on the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, circular reasoning would necessarily follow, as you can see.

Yes, if it is said that the responsible person, after he has believed in the Messenger (ﷺ) and held a firm conviction of his truthfulness in everything that he brought from Allah, exalted is He, in whatever manner that conviction came about, whether by necessity, by reflection, or by taqlid, then he may take his creed from the Qur'an without interpretation and without deviation, without having to examine any rational proof. This would be a sound statement with no objection against it. And it does not entail obtaining what is already obtained, with respect to the matters he first acquired upon which the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, depends. For the second acquisition is from the standpoint that the one who brought their proofs is truthful in them, while the first acquisition was by rational reflection without considering the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So the aspects differ. Let this be understood. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿And Allah knows your moving about﴾ in this world, ﴿and your resting place﴾ in the Hereafter. The "moving about" is specified for this world and the "resting place" for the Hereafter, because everyone is constantly moving in this world toward his return, not stopping, whereas in the Hereafter he is settled and has no movement toward any abode beyond it. The intended meaning of His knowledge, exalted is He, of this is to warn them of His reward and punishment, glorified is He, or to encourage them to comply with what He, majestic is His affair, commands them, and to deter them from what He, mighty and majestic, forbids them, by way of metonymy (kinaya).

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "﴿Your moving about﴾ is your movement in your worldly life, and ﴿your resting place﴾ is your abode in your graves and your Hereafter." 'Ikrima said: "﴿Your moving about﴾ is in the loins of fathers and the wombs of mothers, and ﴿your resting place﴾ is your dwelling on the earth." Al-Tabari and others said: "﴿Your moving about﴾ is your activity in your waking state, and ﴿your resting place﴾ is your sleep." It has also been said: "﴿Your moving about﴾ is in your livelihoods and your trades, and ﴿your resting place﴾ is where you settle from your dwellings." It has been said: "﴿Your moving about﴾ is in your deeds, and ﴿your resting place﴾ is the Garden and the Fire."

Abu Hayyan chose that both terms be general, covering every movement and every dwelling. Similar to this is what has been said: the intended meaning is that He knows all your conditions, so nothing of them is hidden from Him, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Abbas recited (munqalabakum) with a nun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 20:

﴿And those who believe say﴾, eager for jihad because of the great reward in it. So the intended ones are the sincere believers. ﴿"If only a surah had been sent down!"﴾ That is, "Why was a surah not sent down in which jihad is commanded?" So *lawla* here is *tahdidiyyah* (exhortative, expressing urging). It is reported from Ibn Malik that *la* is extra, and the sense is "if a surah had been sent down." But this is not correct.

﴿Then when a decisive surah is sent down and fighting is mentioned in it﴾, that is, by way of command to it. By *muhkamah* (decisive) is meant clear, with no ambiguity or possibility of any meaning other than the obligation of fighting. Al-Zamakhshari explained it as "not abrogated in its rulings." It is reported from Qatadah that every surah in which fighting is mentioned is *muhkamah*, and it is the hardest part of the Qur'an for the hypocrites. This is a matter Qatadah derived from the Qur'an, not specific to this verse. What is established is that the verses about fighting are not abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e. superseded by later revelation), and their ruling remains until the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: *muhkamah* means decisive in matters of the lawful and the unlawful.

It is read *nuzzilat* (with *surah* as the subject) in the passive, from the form *nazala* (the unaugmented triliteral), with *surah* in the nominative as the agent.

Zayd ibn Ali read *nazalat* in the same way, except that he put *surah muhkamah* in the accusative. This is explained by taking the agent as a pronoun referring to the surah, and *surah muhkamah* is then in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*) construction. He and Ibn Umayr read *wa-dhakara* in the active, with its subject being His pronoun, may He be exalted, and *al-qital* in the accusative as its object.

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, hypocrisy. It has been said: weakness in religion. ﴿looking at you with the look of one who has fainted from death﴾, that is, the look of a dying man whose eyes do not blink. The meaning is that their eyes stare out of cowardice and terror. It has been said that they do this out of intense hostility toward him, upon him be blessings and peace. It has also been said that they do it out of fear of exposure, for if they hold back from fighting they will be disgraced and their hypocrisy will become evident.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They used to claim eagerness for jihad and wish for it with their tongues, saying, "If only a surah concerning jihad had been sent down!" But when it was sent down and they were commanded in it to do what they had wished for and had been eager for, they shrank back, it was hard for them, and they were dismayed, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them fear men﴾.

The more apparent reading is what we mentioned at the start, that the speakers are those who were sincere in their faith. What afflicted the hypocrites when the command to the believers to fight was revealed was only because they were included among the believers according to the outward appearance of their state. He (al-Alusi) also permitted that the intended meaning of "those who believe" is a specific group, but his wording clearly favors what he mentioned first. The apparent meaning is that the expression involves the placing of an outward noun in place of a pronoun (*iqamat al-zahir maqam al-mudmar*).

It was also permitted that what is sought in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿If only a surah had been sent down!﴾ is the sending down of a surah in general, since they were comforted by revelation and felt lonely when it was delayed. Something similar is reported from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said concerning the verse: The believers longed for the Book of God, may He be exalted, and for the explanation of what was sent down to them in it. So when a surah was sent down in which fighting was mentioned, "you see, O Muhammad, the hypocrites looking at you," etc.

﴿Woe to them﴾ is a threat and a warning, according to what has been reported from more than one scholar. It is also reported from Abu Ali that *awla* in it is a proper name for the very word *al-wayl* (woe), built on the pattern *af'al* from the word *wayl* by metathesis, and its original form is *awyal*. It is not declined because of its being a proper noun and its pattern. So the sentence is a subject and predicate.

It has been objected that *al-wayl* is not inflected, and that something like *yawm ayyum* (a day of misfortune), although not regularly formed, is never used alone without its qualified noun. Also, metathesis is contrary to the original form and is not resorted to except on evidence. Also, a generic proper name is something outside analogy and is difficult to conceive, especially in the present context. Then it has been said that the clear derivation is from *wali* in the sense of "near," as in the poet's words:

*Layla burdens me, though her close one has become distant,*
*and afflictions and calamities have come between us.*

This points to the fact that it was originally a comparative (*tafdil*), and it became predominant in the sense of nearness to destruction and the invocation of evil. It is as if it were said: "Destruction is nearer for them," meaning "God, may He be exalted, destroy them with a destruction nearer to them than every evil and every ruin." This is like how *bu'dan* (far away) and *suhqan* (ruin) became predominant in the sense of destruction. On this view it is in the accusative as an adjective of an implied verbal noun (*masdar*) which has been put in its place, and the prepositional phrase is attached to it.

In the *Sihah* it is reported from al-Asma'i: *Awla lahu* means that what destroys him has come near him, i.e. has befallen him. He recited:

*So he went on between its two forelimbs, and it was near to exceeding three.*

That is, it came near to exceeding. Tha'lab said: No one has said anything about *awla* better than what al-Asma'i said. On this view it is an implicit verb whose subject is a pronoun for destruction, by the indication of the context. Close to this is what has been said: it is a past-tense verb whose subject is a pronoun for Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and the *lam* is extra, meaning "God, may He be exalted, brought them what they hate," or else the *lam* is not extra, meaning "God, may He be mighty and majestic, brought destruction near to them." The apparent view is that the *lam* is extra, according to what I have heard from al-Asma'i. Whoever explained it as "nearness" permitted both possibilities.

It has also been said that it is an *ism al-fi'l* (verb-noun, a noun functioning as a verb), and the meaning is: "Their protector is evil after evil." It has been said that it is *fa'la* from *ala* in the sense of "return," not *af'al* from *wali*. On this view it is in origin a curse against them, that their affair should return to destruction. The meaning is that God, may He be exalted, destroy them. However, the construction is a subject and predicate.

Al-Radi said: It is a proper name for threat, from *waliyahu al-sharr*, meaning "evil drew near him." The construction is also a subject and predicate. He cited as evidence what Abu Zayd related from their saying *awlaah* with the feminine *ta'*, which shows that it is neither a comparative *af'al* nor a *fa'la* form, and that it is a proper name and not a verb. He then said: Rather it is like *armal* and *armalah* when used as names, and for this reason it is not declined. It is also not a verb-noun, as shown by *awlaah* in the feminine with a nominative ending, meaning that it is inflected. If it were a verb-noun it would be indeclinable like it.

This was objected to on the ground that there is no barrier to *awlaah* being a different word with the same meaning, which does not refute the earlier views at all. It also came first as a comparative and as an adverb like *qabl* (before), and *awlah* was heard with it, as Abu Hayyan reported. It has also been said that the best view is that it is a comparative with the meaning of "more deserving" and "more fitting," and it is the predicate of an implied subject, which is to be understood in each context according to what suits it. The implied element here is: "Punishment is more fitting for them." This was reported from Qatadah, and Ibn Atiyyah inclined to this view. But on all these views...

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 21:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Obedience and honourable speech﴾ is an independent sentence from which one of the two parts is omitted. As for the predicate (khabar), its estimated form is "better for them" or "more fitting," and this is the view of Mujahid and the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. As for the subject (mubtada'), its estimated form is "the matter" or "our matter is obedience," i.e., the matter that is pleasing to God, the Exalted, is obedience. It has been said: that is, their matter is a known obedience, and "honourable speech" means speech whose state is known to be deceit. It has also been said that this is a quotation of their saying before the command to fight, i.e., they said "our matter is obedience," and the reading of Ubayy supports this: (they say, "obedience and honourable speech").

Some scholars held that (awla) is an elative (af'al al-tafdil) functioning as a subject (mubtada'), (lahum) is its complement (silah), and the lam carries the meaning of the ba' (bi-), while (ta'ah) ("obedience") is the predicate (khabar). It is as if it were said: "So more fitting for them than looking at you with the gaze of one who has fainted from death is obedience and honourable speech." Upon this view, it is not an independent sentence, and one does not stop at (lahum). Among what should not be given attention is what has been said: that (ta'ah) is an adjective (sifah) of "surah" in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So when a surah is sent down﴾, and the intended meaning is "possessing obedience" or "obeyed." Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it is worthless because of the large separation between the adjective and the qualified noun.

﴿So when the matter is resolved upon﴾: that is, it became serious (jadd), and the resoluteness (jadd), i.e., striving, belongs to the people of the matter, though it is attributed to the matter figuratively, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, that is of the determined matters﴾. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The war has grown fierce against you, so be earnest."

The apparent view is that the response (jawab) of (idha) is the words of the Exalted: ﴿then if they had been true to God﴾, and it is the governing element of it. The presence of the fa' does not harm this, and it does not prevent what follows from governing what precedes in such a construction, as they have explicitly stated; this is like "when winter comes, then if you came to me I would clothe you." It has been said that the response is omitted, its estimated form being "when the matter is resolved upon, they disliked it," or something similar, as said by Qatadah. In al-Bahr: whoever takes ﴿obedience and honourable speech﴾ to mean that they say this as deceit, estimates: "when the matter is resolved upon, they break their word and disobey." Perhaps whoever makes the earlier saying belong to the believers in outward appearance, namely the hypocrites, also permitted this estimate. Some of them estimated the response as "then be truthful," and this, as you see, is weak. In any case, the intended meaning is: ﴿then if they had been true to God﴾ in what they claimed of eagerness for jihad, and perhaps they displayed eagerness for it as the sincere believers do. It has been said: the saying "obedience and honourable speech" is what is meant, and it has been said: their faith is meant. ﴿It would have been﴾, i.e., the truthfulness, ﴿better for them﴾ than what they committed. This is based on their assumption that there is good in it; otherwise, in reality, there is no good in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 22:

﴿Then, would you perhaps﴾ is an address to those in whose hearts is a disease, by way of iltifat (shift of discourse), to emphasize the rebuke and intensify the reproach. Hal (هَلْ) is used for interrogation, and the original purpose of it is that the report (khabar) enters upon the question about its content, and the performative (insha'i) matter for which 'asa (عَسى) is set is what it indicates by way of report. That is: "Is it then expected of you and awaited ﴿if you turn away﴾" from the affairs of the people and take command over them. So it is from wilaya (governance), and the object is omitted. This was related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-Kalbi. ﴿that you would cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship﴾, through mutual strife over authority and greedy scrambling for the carrion of this world. What is expected is anyone who observes their condition, except Allah, glorified and exalted, since that cannot be attributed to Him, subhanahu. The interrogation, with respect to others than Him, the Exalted, is likewise. The meaning is: given the states known of you that indicate eagerness for the world, in that you were commanded to fight, which is a means to the great reward of Allah the Exalted, yet you disliked it, and what has become manifest in you has become manifest, you are deserving that everyone who tastes you and knows your state should say to you: "O people, what do you see? Is it expected of you, if you turn away, that you would cause corruption on the earth," and so on.

Some interpreters explained tawalla (تَوَلَّى) as turning away from Islam, so the verb is intransitive, meaning: "Would you perhaps, if you turn away from Islam, return to what you were upon in the Jahiliyyah of corruption on the earth through plundering and raiding one another, severing kinship by fighting among relatives against each other, and burying daughters alive?" It was objected that what falls within the conditional in such a context must have its prohibited character considered in terms of the corruptions that follow from it, not in terms of its essence. There is no doubt that turning away from Islam is the head of every evil and corruption, so it is right that it be made the principal element of the rebuke, not a means of rebuking for what is lesser than it of corruptions. The first reading is supported by the reading of some (وُلِّيتُمْ), in the passive voice, and likewise his (peace be upon him) reading, as mentioned in al-Bahr, and it was related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. Ruways and Ya'qub read (تُولِّيتُمْ), also in the passive voice, on the basis that the meaning is: "The people made you their governors and gathered around your leadership," and the intended sense is that you were rulers among them. It was also said: the meaning is "Violent rulers made you their governors, you went out with them and walked under their banner, and by their corruption you became corrupt." Abu Hayyan preferred the explanation as turning away, but he said: the meaning is: "If you turn away from obeying the command of Allah the Exalted in fighting, you will cause corruption on the earth by not aiding the people of Islam against their enemies, and you will sever your ties of kinship, for many of your kin are Muslims; if you do not help them, you sever the kinship between you and them."

It was objected that interpreting corruption as corruption by not giving aid is obscure. Likewise, the use of 'an (أَنْ) rather than idha (إذا) is problematic, since turning away from obeying the command of Allah the Exalted in fighting is almost certain from those hypocrites. So consider this carefully. (﴿and that you would cause corruption﴾) is the predicate (khabar) of 'asa.

﴿And if you turn away﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD), and the response of 'an is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Some claimed that the more apparent view is to make ﴿if you turn away﴾ a circumstantial clause (hal) of anticipated (muqaddara) status. It is objected that a conditional clause without its response has not been known to occur as a circumstantial clause, except with the conjunctive waw (الواو الوصلية), which does not separate from the waw. Attaching pronouns to 'asa as in the rest of the conjugated verbs is the dialect of the people of Hijaz, while the Banu Tamim do not attach them to it, and they require its being followed by 'an and the verb, so they say: "al-Zaydani 'asa an yaquma (the two Zaydans are likely to stand)" and "al-Zaydun 'asa an yaqumu (the Zaydun are likely to stand)." Al-Imam mentioned these two dialects, then said: as for the saying of one who says "'asa anta taqumu (you are likely to stand)" and "'asa ana aqumu (I am likely to stand)," it is inferior to what we have mentioned, because of the prolixity it contains. If his intent is to relate a third dialect, namely the separation of the pronoun, then we do not know of any of the transmitters of the Arabic language who mentioned it; and if it is other than that, then there is not much benefit in it.

Nafi' read (عَسِيتُمْ) with a kasra on the unpointed sin, and this is rare. 'Amr, in one narration, and Salam, Ya'qub, Aban and 'Isma read (تَقْطَعُوا) with the light form, present tense of qata'a. Al-Hasan read (تَقَطَّعُوا) with a fatha on the ta' and the qaf and a shadda on the ta', and its origin is tatqatta'u with two ta's, one of which was deleted. They put (أَرْحامَكُمْ) in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning "in your wombs (kinship ties)," because taqatta'a is intransitive.

[Page 70 of the text]

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the people addressed, using the device of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which signals that mentioning their faults made it proper to remove them from the rank of direct address, even if only as a rebuke, and to report their dreadful sayings to others. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, meaning He removed them far from His mercy, Mighty and Majestic is He, so ﴿He made them deaf﴾ to hearing the truth because they turned deaf to it through their poor choice, and ﴿blinded their sight﴾ because they shut their eyes to the signs displayed before them in themselves and across the horizons. The phrasing is ﴿fa-asamma-hum﴾ (He made them deaf) and does not say "asamma adhanahum" (He made their ears deaf), whereas in the second clause it is ﴿wa-a'mā abṣārahum﴾ (and blinded their sights) and not "wa-a'māhum" (and blinded them), as in the case of ﴿fa-asamma-hum﴾. It has been said that this is because if the ear were struck by cutting or uprooting, speech would still be heard, so there would be no need to mention the ear; and if the sight, which is the eye, were struck, seeing would be impossible. Thus the eye has a role in seeing, while the ear has no role in hearing. End of quotation, and it is as you see.

Al-Khafaji said: Because when deafness is mentioned, there is no need to mention the ears. As for blindness, it is because it is common in the sense of sight and insight (basirah), to the point that it was said it is literally used for both. The evidence of the Qamus supports this. So when one of the two is intended, specifying it is good.

It has also been said, on the basis that blindness is literally of the sight, that expressions like "a'mā Allāh abṣārahum" (Allah blinded their sights) are, outwardly, of the type "abṣartu-hu bi-'aynī" (I saw him with my own eye), which is said in a context needing emphasis. Since the people whose condition He described regarding jihad did not clearly show blindness as they clearly showed deafness, and since in the preceding verses there is what indicates that they did not benefit from what was heard of the Qur'an, which is a result of their deafness, while there is nothing in them indicating that they did not benefit from the visible signs displayed in themselves and across the horizons, which is a result of their blindness, it was fitting to adopt in each of the two clauses what was adopted, along with the observance of the rhyme (fawasil) in the latter, which is more refined than what came before.

Here, "al-arḥām" is the plural of "raḥim" (with a fatha on the rā' and a kasra on the ḥā'), which according to the Qamus means kinship, or its origin and causes. Al-Raghib said: "al-raḥim" is the womb of a woman, that is, the house where her child grows and its container, and from it the word "raḥim" was borrowed for kinship, because they came out of one womb. Relatives are also called "dhawu raḥim," just as they are called "arḥām." Ibn al-Athir explicitly stated that "dhu al-raḥim" applies to everyone with whom you share a lineage, and in the sciences of inheritance (al-fara'id) it is applied to relatives through females. What is mentioned in their books is that it means every relative who is not a sharer (dhu sahm) or an agnatic heir ('asabah), and they counted among these the children of sisters, whether full or paternal, and the paternal aunts of fathers.

The apparent sense of the jurists' words in his, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever owns a dhu raḥim within the forbidden degrees (dhu raḥim muḥarram), he is free" (man malaka dhā raḥimin muḥarramin fa-huwa ḥurrun), indicates that parents and children are included in dhu raḥim linguistically, since they all agreed that they are freed when owned by someone, due to this report, even though they differed on the freeing of others. Ibn Hajar al-Haytami explicitly stated in al-Zawajir that children are among the arḥām. The apparent meaning of the conjunction of "al-aqrabun" (the nearest kin) with "al-walidayn" (the parents) in the verse requires that they are not included among the relatives, so they are not included among the arḥām, since, as they said, they are the "aqārib" (relatives). The words of our jurists are clear that parents and children are not included in this, since they said: If someone bequeaths to his relatives, or to those of his kinship, or to his arḥām, it goes to the nearest then the nearer of every dhu raḥim within the forbidden degrees, and parents and children are not included.

As for grandfathers and grandchildren, Abu al-Su'ud reported from al-'Allama Qasim, from al-Bada'i', that the correct view is that they are not included, and al-Ikhtiyar chose this, and justified it by saying that a relative is one who draws near to another through an intermediary, and the partiality (juz'iyyah) between them is nonexistent. In the commentary of al-Hamawi, their inclusion is the more correct view. In the text of al-Mawahib: Muhammad included the grandfather and the grandchildren (al-hafadah), and this is the apparent view from them both. He also mentioned that the like of the grandfather and grandmother... It may be said that the non-inclusion of parents and children in this, and likewise grandfather and grandchildren according to those who say they are not included, is not because the term does not apply to them linguistically, but because it does not apply to them customarily, and they (the jurists) took custom into account, as al-Tahtawi said in most issues of bequest. In Jami' al-Fusulayn: the general speech among people is understood as what is customary. What he mentioned in al-Mi'raj, from the report of one who named his father "relative" (qarib) and was thereby disobedient to him, does not show that he is not a relative linguistically; rather it is a statement of a legal ruling whose basis is that this causes harm to the parent and lowers his status customarily. This is like one who calls him by his name while he dislikes that.

The matter of the conjunction in the noble verse is easy, because it is permissible to conjoin the general to the specific just as the specific to the general. So what appears preferable to me is that the arḥām, as they explicitly said, are relatives by non-causal kinship (al-qarabah al-ghayr al-sababiyyah), and the intended meaning is what stands opposite to strangers (al-ajanib), and it includes ascendants, descendants and collaterals, on the paternal or maternal side. The prohibition of severing any of them is undoubted, because according to what we have said, each is a raḥim, and the verse is clear in the prohibition of severing the raḥim.

Al-Qurtubi, in his commentary, related the consensus of the community on the prohibition of severing it and the obligation of maintaining it (silah). There should be no hesitation that severing (qat') is a major sin (kabirah). It is strange that al-Rafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, hesitated over the statement of the author of al-Shamil that it is among the major sins, and likewise al-Nawawi, may his secret be sanctified, endorsed his hesitation.

There has been disagreement over the intended meaning of "qati'ah" (severance). Abu Zur'ah said: It should be restricted to harm (isa'ah). Others said: It is the abandonment of kindness (ihsan) even without harm, because the hadiths command maintaining ties and forbid severance, and there is no intermediate between them. Maintaining ties (silah) is the delivery of a type of kindness, as many have explained it, so severance is its opposite, which is the abandonment of kindness.

Al-Haytami objected to this, on the basis that disobedience ('uquq) is explained as doing to one of the two parents what would be forbidden as a minor sin if done to a stranger, so that with respect to one of them it becomes a major sin, and the parents are greater than the rest of the relatives. Then he said: What seems right, to agree with their words and to distinguish between disobedience and severing the raḥim, is that the first means doing to one of the parents what causes them harm, and if that harm is not slight by custom it is a major sin, even if it would not be forbidden if done to someone else. The second means cutting off what the relative was accustomed to receive from the close bond and kindness, without a legitimate excuse, because cutting that causes hearts to be estranged and hurt. So if it is supposed that a relative never received any kindness or harm from him, he does not become a sinner by that, because if this is supposed about the parents without doing to them something that causes great harm, for example through their wealth, it would not be a major sin; so the rest of the relatives are more so.

If it is supposed that a person does not cut off from his relative what he was accustomed to receive of kindness, but he does to him a minor prohibited act, or frowns at him, or does not stand up for him in a gathering and pays him no attention, this is not sinful, unlike with one of the parents, because the emphasis on their rights required that they be distinguished from the rest of the relatives by something that is not found in them. Based on the definition of the second that I have mentioned, there is no difference whether the kindness the relative was accustomed to receive is money, correspondence, messaging, visiting, or otherwise. So cutting all of that after having been doing it, without excuse, is a major sin.

The excuse regarding money should be understood as the lack of what he used to give him, or the renewed need for it, or that the Lawgiver recommends preferring someone other than the relative because that person is more in need or more deserving. So failing to be kind to the relative, or preferring a stranger over him for this excuse, lifts blame from him, even if what the relative was accustomed to receive from him is cut off because of that, since he only observed the command of the Lawgiver to prefer the stranger. It is clear that if a relative was accustomed to receive from him a specific amount of money, for example giving it every year, and he reduced it, he does not become a sinner by that, unlike if he cut it off entirely without excuse.

As for the excuse regarding visiting, it should be delimited by the excuse of Friday prayer, by the shared principle that each is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) and abandoning it is a major sin. As for the excuse for abandoning correspondence and messaging, it is that he cannot find someone trustworthy to deliver what he would send with him. It appears that if he abandons a visit that was customary at a specific time for an excuse, he is not obligated to make it up at a different time.

Children and paternal uncles are among the arḥām, and likewise the maternal aunt, so what has been established regarding the difference between severing them and disobeying the parents applies to them. As for al-Zarkashi's statement: "It is established in a hadith that the maternal aunt is in the position of the mother, and that the paternal uncle of a man is the twin (sinw) of his father," and that its implication is that they are like the father and mother, even in disobedience, this is very far-fetched. It is enough that they resemble them in some respect, such as custody (hadanah), which the maternal aunt has just as the mother has, and likewise the status of being a mahram, and honoring, as with the paternal uncle, and the mahram status and other matters mentioned. End of his statement, the meaning of which is what is intended.

If it were said that a minor sin becomes major if done with a relative, but it is less than what would be so if done with one of the parents, this is not far from my view, because the ugliness of evil deeds varies according to relations. Indeed, it is not far, on this basis, that the ugliness of severing the raḥim varies by consideration of the one who severs and by consideration of the one who is severed. And once variation is granted, it should be said likewise in disobedience, and the disobedience of the mother would be worse than the disobedience of the father, and likewise disobedience toward a child whom one cares for is worse than disobedience toward a child one does not care for, and from this branches out what branches out, as no jurist would miss.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse as evidence for prohibiting the sale of an umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child). Al-Hakim reported it in al-Mustadrak and graded it sahih, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Buraydah, who said: I was sitting with 'Umar when he heard a crier, so he asked, and it was said: A girl from Quraysh is being sold, and her mother is being sold. So he sent for the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and before an hour had passed the house and the chamber were full. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "As to what follows, do you know whether severance (qati'ah) was among what Muhammad, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, brought?" They said: "No." He said: "It has indeed become widespread among you," then he recited: ﴿Would you, if you were to turn away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ Then he said: "And what severance is greater than that the mother of a man be sold among you?" They said: "Do what you see fit." So he wrote to the regions that the mother of a free person must not be sold, for that is severance of kinship, and it is not lawful.

It was also used as evidence for the permissibility of cursing Yazid with what he deserves from Allah, the Exalted. Al-Barzanji in al-Isha'ah and al-Haytami in al-Sawa'iq reported that when his son 'Abd Allah asked Imam Ahmad about cursing Yazid, he said: "How would one not curse him whom Allah, the Exalted, cursed in His Book?!" 'Abd Allah said: "I have read the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and I did not find the cursing of Yazid in it." The Imam said: "Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Would you, if you were to turn away, cause corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship? - It is those whom Allah has cursed...﴾ (the verse)." And what corruption and severance is worse than what Yazid did? End of quotation.

This is based on the permissibility of cursing a specific sinner from among a group that has been cursed by description. On this there is disagreement. The majority hold that it is not permissible to curse a specific person, whether he is a sinner or a dhimmi, living or dead, and whose death upon disbelief is not known, because there is the possibility that he may end his life in Islam, or has ended his life in Islam. This differs from one whose death upon disbelief is known, such as Abu Jahl.

Shaykh al-Islam al-Siraj al-Bulqini held that it is permissible to curse a specific sinner, based on the hadith in the two Sahihs (the two collections of authentic hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim): "If a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses to come, and he spends the night angry, the angels curse her until morning." In another narration: "If a woman spends the night forsaking her husband's bed, the angels curse her until morning."

The possibility that the angels' cursing of her (peace be upon them) is not specific but general, by saying, "God's curse upon whoever spends the night forsaking her husband's bed," is remote, even though his son al-Jalal al-Bulqini discussed it with him.

In al-Zawajir: If one were to argue for this from the report of Muslim, "that he (ﷺ) passed by a donkey that had been branded on its face, and said: God curses whoever did this," it would be more evident, since the demonstrative "this" is explicit in cursing a specific individual, unless it is interpreted as meaning the category. And there is what there is in it. End of quotation.

On this view there is no hesitation in cursing Yazid, given the abundance of his wicked attributes and his committing grave sins throughout the days of his legal responsibility. What he did during his days of dominance over the people of Medina and Mecca suffices. Al-Tabarani narrated with a good chain (sanad hasan): "O God, whoever wrongs the people of Medina and frightens them, frighten him, and upon him is the curse of God, of the angels and of all people; no repentance (sarf) or ransom ('adl) will be accepted from him."

The greatest calamity is what he did to the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt), his approval of the killing of al-Husayn, may peace be upon his grandfather and him, his rejoicing at that, and his humiliation of his family. The meaning of these is mutawatir (reported by so many chains that its truth is certain), though its details are solitary reports (ahad).

In a hadith: "Six I have cursed, and in a version: God has cursed them, and every prophet whose supplication is answered: the one who distorts the Book of God, and in a version: the one who adds to the Book of God; the one who denies the decree of God; the one who domineers with tyranny to exalt whom God has abased and to abase whom God has exalted; the one who makes lawful what is forbidden from my family (itrah); and the one who abandons my Sunnah."

A group of scholars definitively declared him a disbeliever and explicitly cursed him, among them the hafiz (memorizer and master of hadith) Nasir al-Sunnah Ibn al-Jawzi, and preceding him was al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. The allamah al-Taftazani said: "We do not hesitate about his status; rather, about his faith. The curse of God be upon him and upon his supporters and helpers." Among those who explicitly cursed him was al-Jalal al-Suyuti, may God have mercy on him.

In Tarikh Ibn al-Wardi and the Kitab al-Wafi bil-Wafayat: when the captives arrived from Iraq to Yazid, he went out and met the children and women of the descendants of Ali and al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both, while the heads were on spear points, and they had reached the Pass of Jayrun. When he saw them, a crow cawed, and he improvised, saying:

When that caravan appeared and those heads overlooked the cliff of Jayrun,
the crow cawed, so I said: say, or do not say,
for I have exacted my debts from the Messenger.

He meant that he had avenged those whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) killed on the day of Badr, like his grandfather Utba, his maternal uncle, the son of Utba, and others. This is clear disbelief. If it is authentically from him, then he disbelieved by it. Similar is his quoting the verses of Abd Allah ibn al-Zib'ara before his conversion to Islam: "Would that my elders..." (the verses).

Al-Ghazali, may God forgive him, issued a fatwa (legal ruling) on the prohibition of cursing him.

Al-Saffarini, a Hanbali, criticized the report of al-Barzanji and al-Haythami cited earlier from Ahmad (may God have mercy on him), saying: "The position preserved from Imam Ahmad is contrary to what those two reported. In al-Furu' is what its text says: 'Among our companions is one who excluded al-Hajjaj from Islam, so Yazid and the like would be similarly [excluded].' Ahmad's text is contrary to that, and the companions follow it. Cursing by specification is not permitted, contrary to Abu al-Husayn, Ibn al-Jawzi and others." Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyya) said, and God knows best: "The apparent statement of Ahmad is disapproval." I say: the preferred view is that of Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Husayn al-Qadi, and whoever agreed with them. End of al-Saffarini's words.

Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi al-Maliki, upon him be from God what deserves the greatest slander, claimed that al-Husayn was killed by the sword of his grandfather (ﷺ), and he has followers among the ignorant in this. "Great is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say only a lie." (Qur'an 18:5)

Ibn al-Jawzi, may God have mercy on him, said in his book al-Sirr al-Masun: "Among the common beliefs that prevailed among a group claiming adherence to the Sunnah is that they say Yazid was upon the right course and that al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him, erred in rising against him. If they looked into the biographies, they would know how the pledge of allegiance was made to him and how he obliged people to it, and he committed every ugliness in that. Then, even if we assume the validity of the pledge, there appeared from him things all of which necessitate its annulment. No one inclines to that except every ignorant commoner of a sectarian bent who thinks he thereby enrages the Rafidites (Shi'ites, in polemical usage).

"All of this, and what he mentioned, makes clear the people's disagreement about him. Some say he is a Muslim sinner for what proceeded from him along with the pure family, but cursing him is not permitted. Some say he is likewise, and cursing him is permitted, with or without disapproval. Some say he is a disbelieving accursed one. Some say he did not sin by that and cursing him is not permitted, and the one who says this should be placed in the line of Yazid's supporters.

"I say: what predominates on my assumption is that the wretch did not believe in the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that the totality of what he did with the people of God's sanctuary, the people of His Prophet's sanctuary, and his pure and good family, in life and after death, and the disgraces that proceeded from him, is no weaker an indication of his non-belief than throwing a page of the noble Mushaf into filth. I do not think his affair was hidden from the eminent Muslims at that time, but they were overpowered and subdued, and could do nothing but be patient, so that God would decree a matter that was to be done.

"Even if it is granted that the wretch was a Muslim, he is a Muslim who combined grave sins that speech cannot encompass. I go to the permissibility of cursing the like of him specifically, even if it cannot be imagined that there is a like of him among the wicked. The apparent is that he did not repent, and the possibility of his repentance is weaker than his faith. Ibn Ziyad, Ibn Sa'd and a group join him, so the curse of God, mighty and majestic, be upon them all, and upon their supporters, helpers, partisans, and whoever inclined to them until the Day of Religion, for as long as an eye wept over Abu Abd Allah al-Husayn.

"The verse of the poet of the age, possessor of clear merit, Abd al-Baqi Efendi al-Umari al-Mawsili, pleases me, when he was asked about cursing the accursed Yazid:

Yazid's share of my curse is broad in its scope,
so I shall continue to curse him with curses for all time.

Whoever fears blame and talk from explicitly cursing that misguided one, let him say: 'God, mighty and majestic, curses whoever was pleased with the killing of al-Husayn, and whoever harmed the family of the Prophet (ﷺ) without right, and whoever usurped their rights,' for he is a curser of him by entering under the general in the first place, in reality. No one disagrees about the permissibility of cursing with these words and the like, except Ibn al-Arabi mentioned above and his followers, for they, according to what is reported from them, do not permit cursing whoever was pleased with the killing of al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him. By my life, that is the far-reaching error that nearly exceeds the error of Yazid."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 24:

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ That is: they do not take note of it, nor do they peruse it and what it contains of admonitions and warnings, so that they would not fall into the destructive sins into which they have fallen. ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ This is a figurative expression for the non-arrival of the reminder at them and the non-disclosure of the matter to them. It is as if it were said: "Will they not reflect upon the Qur'an once it has reached their hearts, or has it not reached them?" Thus "am" (or) is connected (muttasilah) according to the view of Sibawayh, and the apparent sense of some people's words favours this.

Abu Hayyan and a group [of scholars] held that it is disconnected (munqati'ah), and that what it carries of the meaning of "bal" (rather) is for transition from the rebuke for not reflecting to the rebuke for their hearts being locked, not accepting reflection or contemplation. The hamzah is for affirmation (taqrir). The indefiniteness of "hearts" (qulub) serves to magnify their condition and to make monstrous their state and affair in hardness and ignorance, as if it were said: "upon hearts, unknown, whose condition cannot be recognised and whose extent in hardness cannot be measured." It has also been said that, since what is meant is the hearts of some of them, namely the hypocrites, their indefiniteness is for partitiveness (tab'id) or for classification (tanwi'), as has been said. The annexation of "locks" (aqfal) to it indicates that these are locks specific to them, suited to them, not of the same kind as the other known locks. It has been read as "iqfaluha" with a kasrah on the hamzah, which is a verbal noun (masdar) from the verbs, and as "aqfaluha" in the plural on the pattern af'ul.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾ means they returned to what they had been upon of disbelief. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: it was revealed concerning hypocrites who had embraced Islam and then their hearts became hypocritical. In Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim (Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim, the commentary of Abu al-Suʿud), they are the hypocrites who were described earlier by the sickness of their hearts and other ugly conditions, for they had disbelieved in him (ﷺ). ﴿after guidance had become clear to them﴾ through the manifest proofs and the dazzling, overpowering miracles.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and a group reported from Qatadah that he said: they are the enemies of Allah, the People of the Book, who recognize the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and find him written in the Torah and the Gospel, and then they disbelieve in him (ﷺ). Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij that he said: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back﴾ and so on: the Jews turned back from guidance after they had known that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a prophet. The preferred view is what has preceded. In any case, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the ism of inna (the noun of inna), and the clause ﴿Satan has made it seem fair to them﴾ is its predicate (khabar), as in your saying: inna Zaydan ʿAmrun marra bihi (indeed Zayd, ʿAmr passed by him). That is: he made easy for them the mounting of great sins. From al-sawal, with two fathas, which is looseness, it was used metaphorically for facilitation, meaning he regarded it as easy and light so that it is not heeded, as if it were compared to loosening what had been tied. It was also said: it means inciting them toward desires, from al-sawal, which is wishing. Its origin is driving them toward their sul, that is, what they desire and wish for. Thus the form taʿfil (intensive/causative form) here means driving toward the verbal noun, like gharraba (to make someone a stranger) when he drove him to estrangement, except that they made the verbal noun carry the meaning of the passive participle. This is transmitted from Ibn al-Sikkit.

It has been objected that al-sawal in the sense of wishing derives from al-suʾal (asking), so it is hamzated, whereas al-taswil is from a weak root (waw) and means embellishment; so there is no connection either in form or meaning, and deriving sawwala from it is an error. It has been answered that al-sawal derives from al-suʾal and has two usages: it is hamzated, which is the well-known form, and it is weak (with waw or yaʾ), as one says sa'ala yas'alu like khafa yakhafu. They said from it: yatasawalan with waw. So it is permissible that taswil derives from sawal according to this dialect. Or it is according to the well-known form, lightened by changing the hamza, and then this was made obligatory. Its parallel is tadayyara from al-dar (the house), for the continuation of the change in diyar, and likewise tahayyaza for the continuation of the change in hayyiz. The resulting meaning according to this is driving them toward desires.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read ﴿suwwila lahum﴾ in the passive voice. This was explained by assuming an omitted noun: the scheming of Satan made it seem fair to them. It was also permitted to assume: his scheming made it seem fair to them, so the noun was omitted and the pronoun in the genitive took its place, becoming raised and concealed (in the verb). It was said: this is preferable, because it is an assumption made at the time of need. But it is not hidden that the first is less strained.

﴿and has given them respite﴾ means Satan extended for them in hopes and expectations. The meaning of extension in them is widening them and making them extended in themselves or in their time, by whispering to them: you will attain such and such in the world, things that have no basis, so that he hinders them from action. The root of imla' (giving respite) is leaving someone to remain for a long period (milawah min al-dahr, that is, a stretch of time). From this it is said: the meaning is that he promised them long life. Some made the subject of amla (he gave respite) a pronoun for Allah, and the meaning would be: He gave them time and did not hasten punishment upon them. But this involves a disjunction (tafkik), though it was supported by the reading of Mujahid, Ibn Hurmuz, al-Aʿmash, Sallam, and Yaʿqub: (wa-umli) with the hamza of the first person, the present tense of amla, so the subject is then the pronoun for Allah according to the apparent meaning. The basic principle is the agreement of the two readings. It was also permitted that it be a past passive of the augmented form, with its final vowel dropped for lightness, as they said in baqiya (to remain): baqiya with a sukun on the yaʾ.

According to the apparent reading, it was permitted that the waw be resumptive (istinaf, beginning a new clause) and that it be circumstantial (hal, indicating a state). A subject is assumed after it, that is, ﴿wa-ana umli lahum﴾ (and I give them respite), so that it is not anomalous, like qumtu wa-asukku wajhahu (I stood up and I struck his face). The circumstantial reading was also permitted in the reading of the majority, by making the subject the pronoun for Allah, and then qad (indeed) is assumed before it according to the well-known view. Ibn Sirin, al-Jahdari, Shaybah, Abu ʿAmr, and ʿIsa read (wa-umliya) in the passive voice. Then ﴿lahum﴾ is the deputy subject (naʾib al-fail), meaning: they were given respite and their lifespans were extended. It was also permitted that the subject be a pronoun for Satan, and the meaning would be: Satan was given respite for them, that is, he was made one of those granted respite until the Day of Resurrection on their account. In this there is a statement of the continuation of their misguidance and a condemnation of their state.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their apostasy, not to the respite (al-imla') as reported from al-Wahidi, nor to the enticement (al-taswil) as has been said, because neither of them is a consequence of the statement that follows. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the words of the Exalted: ﴿because they said﴾, i.e., on account of their saying, ﴿they﴾, meaning the hypocrites, ﴿to those who detested what Allah had sent down﴾. These were the Jews of Banu Qurayzah and Banu al-Nadir, who detested the descent of the Qur'an upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while knowing that it was from Allah, out of envy and in hope that it would be sent down to one of them. ﴿We will obey you in part of the matter﴾, i.e., in some of your affairs and circumstances. This is what is related of them in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieved: "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you"?﴾ It has also been said: "in some of what you command, such as supporting one another against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And it has been said: the speakers are the Jews who disbelieved in him (ﷺ) after they found his noble description in their scripture, and those addressed are the hypocrites, for the Jews used to promise them support if they openly declared enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It has also been said: the speakers are those Jews and those addressed are the polytheists, who likewise had been promised support by them if they waged war. Both of these views have been objected to: the disbelief of the Jews in him (ﷺ) was not caused by this statement, even if it were supposed to have been uttered by them according to the view of the one who holds it, but rather by their denial of his mission (ﷺ), although they recognized him as they recognized their own sons and fathers. From this it becomes clear what is wrong with the view of some of them that the speakers are the hypocrites and the Jews and those addressed are the polytheists. What we have explained of the noble verse is narrated from the great scholar (al-Habr), may Allah be pleased with him. ﴿And Allah knows their secret dealings﴾, i.e., their concealment of what they say to the Jews, or every ugly thing, and this enters first and foremost. Al-Jumhur read (asrarahum) with an opening hamza, meaning: He knows the things they keep secret, and among them is their saying:
