This is what He, glory be to Him, made manifest in order to expose them. The Imam said: "The more apparent view is to say that the intended meaning is that He, glory be to Him, knows what is in their hearts of knowledge of the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ)." There is in this what is not hidden. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) confirming what precedes it and containing a warning (wa'id),

The fa' in His words, glorified is He, ﴿So how will it be when the angels take their souls﴾, indicates that what follows is connected to what precedes it. "Kayfa" (how) is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted that is the operator of the temporal clause (al-zarf). It is as if it were said: they do in their lives what they do of tricks, so how will they act when the angels take their souls? It was also said that it is in the nominative, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: so how will their state or their trickery be when the angels take them, and so on. Al-Tabari claimed that the implied meaning is: so how will His knowledge of their secrets be when the angels take them, and so on, but this is nothing. The time of the taking (tawaffi) is the time of death, and "the angels" (peace be upon them) are the Angel of Death and his assistants. Al-A'mash read "tawaffahum" with an alif in place of the taa', which allows it to be a past tense verb or a present tense verb from which one of its two taa's has been dropped, the original being "tatawaffahum." ﴿They strike their faces and their backs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the angels. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿took them﴾, but Abu Hayyan considered this weak. It is, as has been said, a depiction of their being taken in the most dreadful and horrific manner, and a making manifest of what they fear and what makes them shrink from fighting, since striking the faces and backs in battle and jihad is among what is avoided.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that no one dies in a state of disobedience except that the angels strike his face and his back. The speech is, in his view, to be taken literally, and there is no obstacle to this, even if those present do not perceive the striking, and this is no different from the questioning of the two angels and the other conditions of the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection).

As for what is meant by the face and the back, it was said that they are the two well-known organs. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid that he said: "They strike their faces and their posteriors, but Allah, glorified is He, is generous and uses euphemism." Al-Raghib and others said that what is meant is the front and the rear. It was also said that the time of taking is the time of their being driven to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and the angels are then the angels of punishment. It was also said that it is the time of fighting, and the angels are angels of victory who strike their faces if they stand firm and their backs if they flee, as support for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Both of these opinions, as you see, are weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 28:

﴿That﴾ – this terrible turning away – ﴿is because﴾ – that is, because of the fact that – ﴿they followed what angered Allah﴾, namely disbelief and sins, ﴿and they disliked His pleasure﴾, that is, what the Mighty and Majestic One is pleased with of faith and acts of obedience, inasmuch as they disbelieved after having believed and departed from obedience through what they did in dealing with their Jewish brethren. It has also been said: ﴿"what angered Allah"﴾ is the concealing of the description of the Messenger (ﷺ), and His pleasure is what pleases Him, glorified is He, of making that manifest. This is based on the view that what precedes is a report about the Jews, and you have heard what is in it. Since following what angers Allah the Exalted entails turning towards [the thing], it is fitting to strike the face [with the verb]; and since disliking His pleasure, glorified is He, entails turning away, it is fitting to strike the back. Thus there is in the speech a parallelism resembling the device of *laff wa nashr* (folding and unfolding). ﴿So He made void﴾ for that reason ﴿their deeds﴾ which they performed while they were believers, of acts of obedience. It is also permissible that what is meant is the acts of righteousness they did afterwards, which, had they performed them while believing, would have benefited them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 29:

﴿Or do those in whose hearts is a disease suppose﴾ are the hypocrites, whose base conditions were detailed. They were described by their earlier attribute, because it is the basis for what was condemned of them in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah will never bring out their rancor﴾. So *am* is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive, meaning "or" introducing a new question), and *an* is *mukhaffafah* (the lightened form of *inna*), its noun being a pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), and the sentence after it is its predicate. *Al-aḍghān* is the plural of *ḍighn*, which means resentment (*al-ḥiqd*). Al-Raghib restricted it to intense resentment. One says *ḍaghina* (with kasra) and *taḍāghana al-qawm* and *iḍṭaghanū*, meaning they concealed their grudges. It is also said: *iḍṭaghantu al-ṣabiyy* when you take the child under your armpit. Al-Ahmar recited:

*As if he were holding a child under his arm*
*And a horse that is resentful, giving nothing of its running except when struck.*

The root of the word is *al-ḍaghan*, which is twisting and bending in the legs of an animal, in a spear shaft, and in everything. Bishr said: "Like the one with a twisted leg walking over the stony ground." Al-Layth recited:

*Indeed my spear is among the hard spears,*
*Which the straightening has only made more crooked.*

The resentment in the heart is likened to this. Al-Layth and Qutrub said: *al-ḍaghan* is enmity. The poet said:

*Say to the son of Hind what you intended by your speech,*
*Which displeased the friend and increased the grudges.*

This does not contradict the first meaning, because resentment is enmity concerning a matter that a person hides in his heart. *Ikhraj* (bringing out) is specific to physical bodies, and what is meant here is *ibraz* (manifesting). The meaning is: rather, do those in whose hearts is resentment and enmity toward the believers suppose that Allah, exalted is He, will not bring their grudges forth and reveal them to the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and the believers, so that they remain concealed? The sense is that this is something that scarcely falls within the realm of possibility.

**[Verse 47:30]** ﴿And if We willed﴾ to show you them, ﴿We would have shown them to you﴾, that is, We would have made them known to you. This is on the basis that the seeing is of knowledge (*'ilmiyya*). ﴿So you would recognise them by their marks﴾ is a consequence of his (ﷺ) recognition being based on Allah's (Mighty and Majestic) making him know them. It is also permissible for the seeing to be visual, meaning that he (ﷺ) recognises them with a recognition that follows from his being shown them. The shift to the "nun of majesty" (*nun al-'azama*, the first-person plural of majesty) indicates care for the showing. *Al-simā* means the mark. The meaning here is plural because the word is in the construct form, yet it is stated in the singular to indicate that their marks are of one kind, so they are as one thing. That is, ﴿you would recognise them by marks We would brand them with﴾. The *lam* in ﴿so you would recognise them﴾ is the *lam* of the answer (*lam al-jawab*) that occurs in ﴿We would have shown them to you﴾, which follows *law* (if), because what is conjoined to the answer is itself an answer. It is repeated in the conjoined clause for emphasis.

As for the *lam* in His, exalted is He, statement ﴿And you will surely know them by the manner of their speech﴾, it occurs in the answer to an omitted oath, and the clause is conjoined to the conditional clause. *Lahn al-qawl* (the manner of speech) is one of its styles in general, or it is speech that inclines away from the familiar way, that is, it turns away from its apparent sense from plain statement to allusion and ambiguity. For this reason, a grammatical error is called *lahn* (*lahn al-i'rab*), because it deviates from what is correct. Al-Raghib said: *al-lahn* is turning speech away from its customary course, either by removing the *i'rab* (grammatical inflection) or by distortion (*tasḥif*), and this is the blameworthy kind and is more commonly used. Or it is turning it away from explicitness and redirecting its meaning toward allusion and implication, and this is praiseworthy from the standpoint of eloquence. He alluded to this in the words of the poet, which most men of letters cite:

*A sound and correct speech, yet at times you speak with allusion,*
*and the best of speech is that which is allusive.*

It was this that was meant by His, exalted is He, statement ﴿And you will surely know them by the manner of their speech﴾. In *al-Bahr* it is said: *lahantu lahu* (with a fatha on the ḥā') *alhanu lahnan* means I spoke to him a speech which he understands from you while it remains hidden from others. *Lahinahu* (with a kasra) means he understood it, and *alhantuhu* means I made him understand it. *Lāḥantu al-nās* means I was subtle with people. It was also said: *lahn al-qawl* is departing from what is correct. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿the manner of speech﴾ here is their saying, "What do we gain if we obey, in terms of reward?" and they do not say, "What is upon us if we disobey, in terms of punishment?" This is what they ought to have said. Some of those who explained it as the style that inclines away from the familiar way said: they would agree among themselves upon expressions by which they addressed the Messenger (ﷺ), whose apparent meaning was good while they intended something ugly. They also used to speak in words that suggested following, while they were the opposite of that, such as their saying, when the believers called them to help them, "We are with you." In sum, they spoke in words full of deceit, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would recognise them by that.

From Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): after this verse, nothing of the hypocrites remained hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he (peace be upon him) would recognise them by their marks. We were once on some campaign in which there were nine hypocrites whom people complained about. They slept one night, and in the morning, written on the forehead of each of them was: "This is a hypocrite."

As for his claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recognise them by their marks, there is a difficulty, for the apparent sense of *law* (if) is non-occurrence. Rather, what suits the context is that they would be recognised from the manner of their speech. It seems he understood it as a promise of occurrence which indicates impossibility regarding what has passed. It has indeed been confirmed, and it was witnessed in some campaigns. The marks are not confined to writing, but may be other things too, by which the Prophet (ﷺ) recognised them, just as the *qā'if* (tracker, one who reads signs) recognises a person's condition through signs that indicate him. A person often recognises his lover and his hater from looking, and a look almost speaks what is in the heart. We have seen more than one person recognise a Sunni from a Shi'i by features in the face. If it is true that some of the saints, may their secrets be sanctified, used to recognise the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, and would say: "I smell the scent of obedience from so-and-so, the scent of disobedience from so-and-so, the scent of faith from so-and-so, the scent of disbelief from so-and-so," then the matter becomes clearer, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indicated, with that recognition, is more fitting and more fitting. Perhaps it is by signs beyond the scope of our intellects. The light mentioned in the report "Beware of the *firasa* (discernment) of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah, exalted is He" varies in clarity according to capacities, and the Prophet (ﷺ) possessed its fullest measure.

Some have mentioned among the signs of hypocrisy the hatred of 'Ali (may Allah honour his face). Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud who said: "We did not recognise the hypocrites in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except by their hatred of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." He and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri something that supports it. In my view, his hatred (may Allah be pleased with him) is among the strongest signs of hypocrisy. If you accept this, then alas, what would you say about Yazid the accursed? Did he love 'Ali (may Allah honour his face), or did he hate him? I do not think you doubt that the accursed one (upon him be the curse) hated him (may Allah be pleased with him) with the utmost hatred, and likewise he hated his two sons al-Hasan and al-Husayn, upon their grandfather, their parents, and them be blessings and peace, as the widely transmitted reports indicate in meaning. In that case there is no room for you to say that the accursed one was a hypocrite. Indeed, the authentic hadiths mention signs of hypocrisy other than those mentioned, such as his (peace be upon him) saying: "The signs of the hypocrite are three," and the hadith continues.

But the scholars said: these are signs of practical hypocrisy (*nifaq 'amali*), not of hypocrisy of belief (*nifaq i'tiqadi*). It was also said: the hadith is issued in the form of warning against a sincere believer's being characterised by any of them, because at that time they were among the signs of the hypocrites.

The statement of His, exalted is He, ﴿And you will surely know them by the manner of their speech﴾ has been used as evidence that allusive slander (*ta'rid bil-qadhf*) requires the *ḥadd* (fixed punishment). Its status is not hidden. ﴿And Allah knows your deeds﴾, so He will recompense you for them according to your intention. This, as it has been said, is a promise to the believers and an announcement that their state is contrary to that of the hypocrites. It has also been said: it is a threat to the hypocrites and an announcement to them that what is requited is what they intend, not what they hint at or equivocate about. It has been inferred that it is a general address, so it is both promise and threat, and it has been understood in its generality.

"The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely test you﴾ by commanding jihad and similar arduous obligations, ﴿until We know those of you who strive and are patient﴾ over the hardships of the obligations, with a practical knowledge (ʿilm fiʿlī) upon which reward depends. Something to this effect has been said, namely: until Our knowledge becomes manifest. Ibn al-Hajib said regarding this: 'Knowledge is applied on the basis of seeing, and a thing is not seen until it occurs,' meaning according to the well-known view. Here it carries that meaning, or the meaning of recompense, and the sense is: until We recompense those of you who strive and are patient. ﴿And We will test your reports﴾, so that their good and their bad become apparent. The expression is a metonymy for testing their deeds, for the report, whether good or bad, follows what it reports on; so when the good is distinguished from the bad report, the thing reported on, which is the deed, is likewise distinguished. This is more eloquent than 'We will test your deeds.' The apparent meaning is the generality of reports. It is also permitted that the intended meaning is their reports about their faith and their allegiance to the believers, with the idafah (construct) being to a specific referent, i.e., 'and We will test the reports of your faith and your allegiance,' so that their truthfulness and falsehood become apparent.

Abu Bakr read the three verbs whose subject is the pronoun of majesty with the letter yāʾ (yabluwa / yaʿlamu forms as ʿazamah). Ruways read ﴿wa-nabluwa﴾ with nūn and a sukūn on the wāw, and al-Aʿmash read it with a sukūn on the wāw and with yāʾ. In that case the verb is marfūʿ with a presumed ḍammah, according to the estimate 'and We are testing,' and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also permitted that it be manṣūb as in the reading of the majority, its vowel having been dropped for lightness, as in the verse:

"Allah refused that I should be named after mother or father."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 32:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and barred [others] from the way of Allah and opposed the Messenger﴾ became in a opposition other than his opposition, and what is meant is: they opposed him,
صفحة 79
﴿after guidance had become clear to them﴾, either because of what they witnessed of his description (peace and blessings be upon him) in the Torah, or because of the miracles that appeared at the hands of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the signs that were revealed to him (peace and blessings be upon him). They were the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, or the people who fed [others] on the day of Badr, whose mention has already passed. It was also said: they were people who became hypocrites after having believed. ﴿They will not harm Allah﴾ by their disbelief and their barring [others], ﴿in anything﴾, of all things, or [in anything] of harm; or [it means] they will not harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by opposing him in anything. The genitive noun (al-mudaf) has been omitted to exalt him (peace and blessings be upon him), by making his harm and what befalls him like that which is attributed to Allah the Exalted. In this is a severe depiction of their opposition to him (may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace).

﴿And He will nullify their deeds﴾ in their schemes which they set up to invalidate His religion, the Exalted, and to oppose His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). So they will not attain by them what they were seeking of mischiefs, and they will yield nothing for them except killing and exile from their homelands, and the like of that. It is also permitted that what is meant is their deeds which they performed in their religion, hoping thereby for reward.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 33:

﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds.﴾ It is said: The tribe of Banu Asad embraced Islam and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We have preferred you, and we have come to you with our selves and our families," as if they were conferring a favour by this. So this verse was revealed concerning them, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam﴾. From here it is said: the meaning is, do not invalidate your deeds by making a favour of Islam. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: by showing off and seeking reputation. And also from him: by doubt and hypocrisy. And it is said: by self-admiration ('ujb), for it consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood. And it is said: the intended meaning of "deeds" is charities, i.e., do not invalidate them by reminding of them and by harm. And it is said: do not invalidate your acts of obedience by your acts of disobedience. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that he said concerning the verse: "Whoever among you is able not to invalidate a righteous deed by an evil deed, let him do so; there is no power except with Allah, Exalted is He." 'Abd ibn Humayd and Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi reported it in the Book of Prayer. And Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to regard that with "There is no god but Allah" no sin harms, just as with polytheism no deed benefits, until this was revealed: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds﴾, so they feared that sin would invalidate the deed. The wording of 'Abd ibn Humayd is: they feared that the major sins would cause their deeds to be annulled. Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We, the community of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), used to consider that no good deed is unaccepted, until this verse was revealed: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and do not invalidate your deeds﴾. When this verse was revealed we said: What is this that invalidates our deeds? We said: The major sins that necessitate punishment and the grave immoralities. So whenever we saw someone who had committed any of them we said: He has perished. Until this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾. When it was revealed we refrained from speaking about that, and whenever we saw someone who had committed any of them we feared for him, and if he had not committed any of them we hoped for him." The Mu'tazilah used the verse as evidence that major sins invalidate acts of obedience; indeed, a single major sin invalidates deeds when persisted in, even if they were as many as the stars of the sky, and they cited reports on that as they cited. In al-Kashf: at this point it is necessary to clarify the discussion by saying: if the Mu'tazilah mean that, for example, adultery committed after the prayer invalidates its reward, then there is no proof for this either by transmission or by reason; rather, both are equal, as the sound hadiths indicate, and the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, suffices as a decisive proof: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾. And if they mean that its punishment may become so great that small good deeds do not balance it, then this is correct, and the discussion then concerns whether to call it "ihbat" (invalidation), and there is no harm in that; but according to us this invalidation is not necessary, whereas according to them it is necessary, and this is based on the permissibility of pardon, which is another question. As for the major sin that is specific to that act, such as self-admiration and the like of reminding and harm after giving charity, it is certainly invalidating by consensus, and the reports transmitted are to be understood accordingly. And whoever does not call it "ihbat" because he makes it a condition for acceptance, and ihbat means that the reward becomes void, and this cannot arise if no reward was established for it, then that is his position; and this is a matter that goes back to terminology. End of quotation, and it is of excellent quality. The repetition of the verb in "and obey the Messenger" is for emphasis on the importance of obeying him, upon him be blessings and peace.

Verily, those who disbelieved and barred [others] from the way of Allah: they refrained from entering Islam and following its path, or they barred people from it. ﴿Then they died while they were disbelievers, so Allah will never forgive them.﴾ It was revealed concerning the people of the well (ahl al-qalib), as has been said, but its ruling is general, as many scholars have said, applying to everyone who dies upon disbelief. This is clear according to the first interpretation of "barred from the way of Allah." As for the second interpretation, it has been said of it: the generality [of the ruling], together with restricting disbelief to barring people from Islam, is open to question. The implication of some of the eminent scholars' words is that the generality holds, because the basis of non-forgiveness is persistence in disbelief, as the stipulation of this condition in the statement suggests. So reflect upon this.

Some of those who uphold the implied meaning (mafhum) have derived from the implication of the verse that Allah, exalted is He, may forgive all the sins of one who does not die upon disbelief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 35:

﴿So do not falter﴾, meaning: when you know that God, exalted is He, will nullify their deeds and punish them, and that He will abandon them in this world and the Hereafter, then do not concern yourselves with them, and do not show weakness. The fa' (فَ) here is fasihah (a connective particle indicating an implied condition), in answer to an implied condition understood from what precedes it. It has also been said that it is for the sequencing of the prohibition upon what came before it, namely the command to obey.

﴿And call to peace﴾ is conjoined to (تَهِنُوا, "falter") and falls within the scope of the prohibition, meaning: do not call the unbelievers to reconciliation out of feebleness and to show incapacity, for that would be giving up what is dignified (iʿṭāʾ al-daniyyah). It is also permitted that it be in the subjunctive by the implied (an, أنْ), so that the verbal noun (al-maṣdar al-maslūk) is conjoined to a verbal noun deduced from what precedes it, like the saying of the poet: "Do not forbid a trait and then do its like."

Al-Kiya deduced from this prohibition that making truce with the unbelievers is forbidden except in cases of necessity, and that abandoning jihad is forbidden except in cases of incapacity.

al-Sulami read (وتَدَّعُوا, "and call"), with the dal doubled, from iddaʿā in the sense of daʿā (to call). In al-Kashshaf, the particle lā is mentioned in this reading, and perhaps that is another transmission.

al-Hasan, Abu Raja', al-A'mash, ʿIsa, Talhah, Hamzah and Abu Bakr read (al-silm), with a kasrah on the sin. ﴿And you are the superior ones﴾, meaning the dominant ones. ʿUluww in the sense of ghalabah (dominance) is a well-known metaphor, and the clause is a circumstantial clause that confirms the meaning of the prohibition and emphasizes the obligation to desist. Likewise the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And God is with you﴾, meaning His helper. For their being the dominant ones and His, Mighty and Majestic, being their helper are among the strongest reasons for avoiding whatever gives the appearance of humiliation and submission.

Abu Hayyan said: It is permitted that both be independent clauses. They first inform that they are the superior ones, which is news of the unseen made manifest by existence, and then it ascends to a higher rank than the one before it, which is God, exalted, being with them. ﴿And He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾. He said: He will not wrong you. It has been said: He will not diminish them. It has been said: He will not waste them, and this is as Abu ʿUbayd said. Al-Mubarrad said: from witartu al-rajul, when you kill for him a slain man from a child, brother or close kinsman, or you strip him of his wealth and take it from him. Al-Zamakhshari said: its reality is that I isolated him from his relative or his wealth, from al-witr, which is the single. So he likened the wasting of the worker's work and the nullifying of his reward to the depriving of the one who is deprived, and it is of eloquent speech. In it here is an indication of the greater kindness of God, exalted, in what it contains. And from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, it is as if he has been deprived of his family and his wealth."

According to what he mentioned, it is apparent that the verb witrah must be construed with the meaning of stripping or the like, so that it transitively takes the second object directly. In al-Sihah, it is stated that it derives from al-tirrah (vengeance), and taking it as the omission of the preposition is also sound, meaning: I made him one whose vengeance is not attained, as if I had diminished him in it, and treated it like "I entered the house," i.e., into it.

Some permitted that (يَتِرُ, "deprive") here be transitive to one object, with (وأعْمالَكم, "your deeds") as a substitute for the pronoun of address, meaning: He will not deprive your deeds of their reward.

The clause, it has been said, is conjoined to the phrase ﴿with you﴾. Although it does not occur as an independent circumstantial clause because it is introduced by the particle of the future, which is incompatible with the present circumstance, as clearly stated by al-ʿAllamah al-Taftazani and others, nevertheless what is not permitted in other contexts is permitted in a subordinate clause. It has also been said: the obstacle to a clause introduced by the future particle serving as a circumstance is that it contradicts the usage transmitted, and otherwise there is no obstacle to its being a presumed circumstance. Moreover, lan may be merely for emphasizing negation. Apparently those who prohibit it base the prohibition on the incompatibility, and when that incompatibility is removed by consideration of one of the two matters, there is no prohibition. But it has been said: the circumstance intended by it is the expression of the state, which is other than the circumstance that is one of the tenses, and the incompatibility lies only between this circumstance and the future. This is like what those who permit the coming of a past clause as a circumstance without qad have said, and what is related to that and what is said about it in the books of grammar. And if the preceding clause is made an independent resumptive clause, there is no difficulty at all in the conjunction.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 47, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, the life of this world is but play and amusement.﴾ It has no permanence and no worth. ﴿And if you believe and fear God, He will give you your rewards.﴾ That is, the reward of your faith and your God-consciousness, which is among the enduring good deeds (*al-baqiyat al-salihat*) for which competitors compete. ﴿And He will not ask you for your wealth.﴾ This is a conjunction (*'atf*) with the answer (*jaza'*) of the condition. The genitive construction (*idafa*) here is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), so the meaning is: if you believe, He will not ask you for all of your wealth, as He takes all the wealth of the disbeliever. There is a fine correspondence (*muqabala*) here with His saying, ﴿He will give you your rewards﴾, as if it were said: He will give you all the rewards and ask of you some of your wealth, namely what He has prescribed of *zakat* (obligatory alms). The statement of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, that is, He does not ask you for much of your wealth; He only asks you for a quarter of a tenth, then "so be generous of soul" (*fa-tayyibu anfusakum*), is an explanation of the resulting meaning. It has also been said: that is, He does not ask you for what is in fact your property, but asks you for what belongs to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, who is in truth its owner, and who is the One who bestows upon you the benefit of it. It has also been said: that is, He does not ask for your wealth because He has any need of it, but so that your spending returns to you. It has also been said: that is, the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, does not ask you for any of your wealth as a wage for conveying the message, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: I ask you no wage for it, and I am not of those who pretend.﴾ The connection of these (sayings) to it is not clear, and some of them also contain what is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 47, verse 37:

﴿If He asks it of you﴾, i.e., your wealth, ﴿and presses you﴾, i.e., He strains you by demanding all of it. Ihfa' (pressing) and ilhaf (importunity) both mean exaggeration and reaching the utmost limit in anything. It is said: "He pressed him in the request (ahfahu fi al-mas'alah)" when he left out nothing of insistence. And "ahfa sharibahu" means he uprooted it and took it completely. The origin of this, as al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said, is from "ahfaytu al-dabbah" (I made the animal barefoot), i.e., I made its hoof worn away, and "ahfaytu al-ba'ir" (I made the camel) having its footpad worn away from walking until it became thin. ﴿you will be stingy﴾ is the response of the conditional clause, and what is meant by stinginess here is refusing to give, since, according to the well-known meaning, it is a natural matter that is not a consequence of the asking. ﴿and He will bring forth your rancors﴾, i.e., your grudges, due to your excessive love for wealth. The pronoun in (yukhrij) refers to God Most High, and it is supported by the reading of Ya'qub, and it is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas as (nukhrij) with a damma on the nun. It is also permissible that the subject be the asking or the stinginess, since it is the cause of bringing forth the rancors, and the attribution in that case is metaphorical. 'Abd al-Warith narrated from Abu 'Amr (wa-yukhriju) with a raf' (nominative vowel), as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), and it is permissible to make the sentence a circumstantial clause (hal) with the implied meaning "wa-huwa yukhriju." Abu Hatim related this from 'Isa. In al-Lawami' (it is related) from 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr (wa-yakhruju) with a ya' with two dots below? (yā' taḥtiyya), with a fatha on it, and a damma on the ra' and the jim, ﴿your rancors﴾ in the nominative as the subject.

And Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Muhaysin, Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil and al-Yamani read ﴿wa-tukhriju﴾ with the feminine ta', and ﴿your rancors﴾ in the nominative. It is also read (wa-yukhraju) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the ra', (your rancors) in the nominative as a substitute for the subject. This is narrated from 'Isa, except that he put a fatha on the jim by implying "an" (that), so the waw is conjunctive over a verbal noun implied in the context, meaning: "let there be your stinginess and the bringing forth of your rancors."

**﴿Here you are, you are these people﴾**: that is, you, O addressees, are these people described by what His words contain, ﴿If He asks you for them﴾ and so on. The sentence is a subject and predicate, and the vocative particle *ha* (the particle of alerting) is repeated for emphasis. His words, glorified be He, ﴿You are called to spend in the way of Allah﴾ and so on, form a resumptive and confirmatory clause (*isti'naf muqarrir wa mu'akkid*) for that, because the essential meaning of the two is the same. Their being called to spend is the asking of wealth from them, and the stinginess of some of them is the meaning of the non-giving mentioned in summary at the beginning. Alternatively, ﴿these﴾ is a relative clause (*silah*) for "these people," on the understanding that it means "those who." The Kufan grammarians (*al-Kufiyyun*) hold that the demonstrative noun is a relative in all cases, whereas the Basran grammarians (*al-Basriyyun*) do not accept the demonstrative as a relative except when it is preceded by the interrogative *ma*, by agreement, or by *man*, the interrogative, according to disagreement. Spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He, is spending that pleases Him, exalted is His station, in every case. It therefore includes maintenance of dependants and relatives, fighting in the cause of Allah, feeding guests, zakat, and other things. It is not restricted to spending for fighting or to zakat alone, as has been said.

**﴿Among you there is one who is stingy﴾**: that is, there are people who are stingy. **﴿And whoever is stingy, he is only stingy against himself﴾**: so the harm of his stinginess does not extend to anyone else. It is said, "I was stingy toward him" (*bakhiltu 'alayhi*) and "I was stingy from him" (*bakhiltu 'anhu*), because stinginess carries the sense of withholding and of restricting the one from whom good is withheld and to whom harm is done. Hence it is appropriate that it be followed by *'an* for the first and by *'ala* for the second. It is evident that whoever withholds good from himself, his harm falls upon himself, so there is no difference between the two expressions in the result. Al-Tibi said: "It is possible to say that he is stingy against himself, in the sense that stinginess proceeds from himself, because the self is the place of stinginess and its source, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿and whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own self﴾." But this, as you see, is weak.

**﴿And Allah is the Rich﴾**, none other than Him, mighty and majestic is He, **﴿and you are the poor﴾**, those who are perfect in poverty. So what He, glorified be He, commands you is for your need of what it contains of benefits, which wisdom does not require to reach you without it. If you obey, it is for your benefit, and if you turn away, it is upon you.

**﴿And if you turn away﴾** is coordinated with His words, glorified be He, "if you believe," that is, if you turn away from faith and piety. **﴿He will replace you with another people﴾**, He will create other people in your place. This is like His words, exalted is He, "He will bring a new creation." **﴿Then they will not be like you﴾** in turning away from faith and piety, but they will be eager for both.

The particle *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in reality, or else the distance of the rank from what came before. The intended people are the people of Persia.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* have narrated, and al-Tirmidhi (and it is a sound hadith according to the condition of Muslim), from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, ﴿And if you turn away﴾ and so on. They said, 'O Messenger of Allah, who are these people who, if we turn away, will be substituted for us and will not be like us?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck the shoulder of Salman, then said: 'This man and his people. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if faith were hung from the Pleiades, men from Persia would reach it.'"

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Jabir, "religion" appears instead of "faith." It has been said that they are the Ansar. It has been said that they are the people of Yemen. It has been said that they are Kindah and al-Nakha'. It has been said that they are the non-Arabs (*'ajam*). It has been said that they are the Romans. It has been said that they are the angels. Taking "people" to mean them is far-fetched in usage. Since the hadith is authentic, it is my school of thought.

There are two opinions as to whether the address is to the Quraysh or to the people of Medina. The apparent view is that it is to those previously addressed, and the conditional clause is not realized. According to al-Kalbi, the condition for the substitution is their turning away, but they did not turn away, so He, glorified be He, did not replace them with others. And Allah knows best.

Among what some masters of the allusive interpretation (*ahl al-ishara*) have said about some verses: ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you﴾. The help of Allah, exalted is He, from the servant is in two ways, in form and in meaning. As for His help in form, it is the support of His religion, exalted is His majesty, by clarifying the proof, explaining it, expounding His obligations and sunnas, manifesting its meanings, secrets and realities, then by striving in it, raising His word, and suppressing His enemies. As for His help in meaning, it is by annihilating the human (*nasut*) in the divine (*lahut*). The help of Allah, glorified be He, to the servant is also in two ways, in form and in meaning. As for His help to the servant in form, it is by sending messengers, sending down books, manifesting miracles and signs, and clarifying the paths to bliss and hellfire; then by commanding the lesser and greater struggle, and granting success in striving in both, seeking His pleasure, mighty and majestic is He. As for His help to him in meaning, it is by annihilating his existence in His existence, glorified be He, through the manifestation of the attributes of His beauty and majesty.

**﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾** points to the garden of the hearts of the masters of realities, who have guarded themselves against all else, exalted and high is He. **﴿Therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾** is the water of spiritual life which has not changed through long duration. **﴿And rivers of milk﴾** is the divine knowledge, which is the nourishment of souls, or the milk of the natural disposition (*fitrah*) upon which He created people, **﴿whose taste does not change﴾** through the sourness of doubts and illusions, or of desires and innovations. **﴿And rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾** is the wine of longing and love:
